113243.m: High voltage reduces losses when transporting electricity.

113244.q: What is the highest voltage in the Swiss transmission grid?
113244.e: The highest voltage level in Switzerland is 380 kilovolts, which is 380,000 volts. There are also lines with 220 kilovolts.
113244.m: The Swiss extra-high-voltage grid runs at 380 kilovolts.

113245.q: Which company operates the Swiss extra-high-voltage transmission grid?
113245.e: Swissgrid is the national grid company. It operates and monitors Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid.
113245.m: Swissgrid operates the Swiss extra-high-voltage grid.

113246.q: Why can a bird sit safely on a single high-voltage line?
a: Its feathers are made of rubber
113246.e: Both feet are on the same wire, so there is almost no voltage difference. It only becomes dangerous if it touches the ground or a second wire at the same time.
113246.m: Without a voltage difference, no current flows through the body.

113247.q: Why must you never fly kites under high-voltage lines?
a: There is a risk of electric shock
The wind is too weak there
113247.e: A kite string can conduct electricity, especially when damp. If it comes close to the line, a deadly electric arc can form.
113247.m: Never fly kites under high-voltage lines.

113248.q: What are the tall steel structures that high-voltage lines hang from called?
113248.e: Pylons hold the conductor cables high above the ground. This keeps a safe distance from people, buildings and trees.

113249.q: What are the insulators on a pylon for?
a: They separate the line and the pylon electrically
113249.e: Insulators made of glass, porcelain or plastic do not conduct electricity. They stop the current flowing through the pylon into the ground.
113249.m: Insulators stop current flowing into the pylon.

113250.q: Instead of on pylons, where are high-voltage lines sometimes laid?
113250.e: Underground cables are invisible in the landscape, but more expensive and complicated. In Switzerland they are used, for example, in sensitive landscapes.
113250.m: High voltage can also flow through underground cables.

113251.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity production came from hydropower in 2024?
113251.e: Hydropower is Switzerland's most important source of electricity. In 2024, according to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, it supplied around 60 per cent of the country's production.
113251.m: Hydropower supplies more than half of Swiss electricity.

113252.q: Which form of the water's energy does a hydroelectric power station use?
113252.e: Water high up has potential energy. As it flows down, this becomes kinetic energy, which turns the turbine.
113252.m: Hydroelectric power stations use the potential and kinetic energy of water.

113253.q: Why does water from a high reservoir in the Alps provide especially much energy?
a: It falls a long way and becomes fast
It is colder than river water
It is cleaner than river water
113253.e: The greater the height of the fall, the more potential energy the water has. At the bottom it hits the turbine at high speed.
113253.m: A big drop means a lot of energy.

113254.q: What is typical of a river power station, for example on the Rhine?
a: A small drop, but a great deal of water
A big drop, but little water
It needs no water at all
It only uses rainwater from the roof
113254.e: A river power station only dams the river by a few metres. In return, a great deal of water flows through the turbines every second.
113254.m: River power stations use lots of water with a small drop.

113255.q: What is an advantage of hydropower over coal-fired power stations?
113255.e: No fuel is burnt when a hydroelectric power station is running. So hardly any carbon dioxide is produced.
113255.m: Hydropower is renewable energy with little CO2.

113256.q: What are the steps for fish called that help them swim past a river power station?
113256.e: A fish ladder is made of small pools with a gentle slope. This lets fish get round the power station going upstream.
113256.m: Fish ladders help fish get past power stations.

113257.q: Which device at the water intake keeps driftwood and leaves away from the turbines?
113257.e: A rack of steel bars catches branches, leaves and rubbish. A cleaning machine removes the material regularly.
113257.m: A trash rack protects the turbines from floating debris.

113258.q: Which factors does the output of a hydroelectric power station mainly depend on?
a: Amount of water and height of the drop
Taste and depth of the water
Fish population and length of the bank
113258.e: The more water per second and the bigger the drop, the more power a station can produce.
113258.m: The output depends on the amount of water and the drop.

113259.q: What does a run-of-river power station use?
a: The water of a mountain lake
113259.e: A run-of-river power station stands right on a river and uses its continuously flowing water. It only dams the river a little.
113259.m: Run-of-river power stations use the water of rivers.

113260.q: What is the drop typically like at a run-of-river power station?
113260.e: Run-of-river power stations usually dam the river by only a few metres. They make up for the small drop with lots of water.
113260.m: Run-of-river power stations have a small drop.

113261.q: When do run-of-river power stations in Switzerland produce the most electricity?
a: In summer, when the snow melts
Only when there is no wind
113261.e: In early summer and summer, rivers carry a lot of water because of melting snow. In winter there is less water.
113261.m: Run-of-river power stations produce a lot of electricity in summer.

113262.q: On which large river on the border with Germany are there several Swiss run-of-river power stations?
113262.e: On the High Rhine between Lake Constance and Basel there are numerous run-of-river power stations, for example at Rheinfelden and Laufenburg.
113262.m: There are many run-of-river power stations on the High Rhine.

113263.q: What is typical of the electricity production of a run-of-river power station?
a: It only runs during the day
113263.e: The river flows all the time, so run-of-river power stations produce constantly. This is called baseload energy.
113263.m: Run-of-river power stations supply electricity constantly.

113264.q: What is the structure called with which a run-of-river power station dams the river a little?
113264.e: A weir dams the river by a few metres. This creates the drop that the power station uses.
113264.m: A weir dams the river for the power station.

113265.q: Why can a run-of-river power station hardly shift its production to other times?
113265.e: The water flows straight through and is hardly stored. So the station produces when the water comes, not when it is needed.
113265.m: Run-of-river power stations can hardly store water.

113266.q: What is the part of a river power station called in which the turbines and generators stand?
113266.e: The turbines and generators are housed in the powerhouse. It is often right next to the weir in the river.
113266.m: Turbines and generators stand in the powerhouse.

113267.q: What is the big advantage of a storage power station?
113267.e: The water is collected in a reservoir. It can then be released when a lot of electricity is needed, for example in winter.
113267.m: Storage power stations supply electricity when it is needed.

113268.q: What is the water called that must stay in a stream below a water intake so that animals and plants survive?
113268.e: The Water Protection Act requires that not all the water is diverted for producing electricity. The required amount is called the residual flow.
113268.m: Residual flow protects life in the stream below an intake.

113269.q: What is the minimum number of water basins a pumped storage power station needs?
113269.e: It needs an upper and a lower basin. Between them, water is pumped up or let down as needed.
113269.m: A pumped storage power station needs an upper and a lower basin.

113270.q: Why are pumped storage power stations built mainly in the mountains?
a: Because there are big height differences between two basins there
Because less electricity is needed there
Because the Sun shines more strongly there
Because water is lighter in the mountains
113270.e: The higher the upper basin is above the lower one, the more energy there is in the water. In the Alps such height differences are found over short distances.
113270.m: Pumped storage power stations need a big height difference.

113271.q: Why is a pumped storage power station not really an energy producer?
a: It uses more electricity than it supplies
113271.e: There are losses when pumping water up and letting it flow back. So the station is above all a giant battery.
113271.m: A pumped storage power station works like a giant battery.

113272.q: What is the place in the mountains called where water is collected for a storage power station?
113272.e: A dam holds the water back in a reservoir. From there it flows through penstocks to the power station.
113272.m: Storage power stations collect water in reservoirs.

113273.q: How does the water get from the reservoir down to the turbines?
113273.e: Penstocks carry the water steeply downhill. At the bottom the water pressure is very high and drives the turbines powerfully.
113273.m: Penstocks bring the water to the turbines.

113274.q: When do the reservoirs in the Alps fill up the most?
113274.e: In summer snow and glaciers melt and the lakes fill up. In winter the water is used when more electricity is needed.
113274.m: Alpine reservoirs fill up in summer.

113276.q: What rises from the large cooling tower of the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113276.e: In the cooling tower, cooling water is cooled by air. Some of it evaporates, and the visible cloud is water vapour, not smoke.
113276.m: Water vapour rises from the cooling tower.

113277.q: What drives the generator that produces electricity at the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113277.e: The heat from the reactor turns water into steam. The steam turns a turbine, and this drives the generator.
113277.m: In a nuclear power station, steam drives a turbine.

113278.q: Which fuel is split in the Gösgen nuclear power station?
113278.e: The fuel rods contain uranium nuclei. When they split, a lot of heat is released, which heats water into steam.
113278.m: In a nuclear power station, uranium nuclei are split.

113279.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station has a greater output than Gösgen?
113279.e: Leibstadt in Aargau is the most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland, with Gösgen in second place.
113279.m: Leibstadt is Switzerland's most powerful nuclear power station.

113280.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity do nuclear power stations such as Gösgen supply together?
113280.e: Together the Swiss nuclear power stations supply about a third of the electricity. Hydropower supplies the largest share.
113280.m: Nuclear power stations supply around a third of Swiss electricity.

113281.q: Why is the Gösgen nuclear power station shut down for a few weeks every year?
a: For maintenance and changing fuel rods
Because nobody needs electricity in summer
So that the Aare becomes clean again
Because the uranium would otherwise freeze
113281.e: During the yearly overhaul, used fuel rods are replaced and parts of the plant are checked. A supervisory authority checks safety at the same time.
113281.m: Nuclear power stations are regularly maintained and inspected.

113282.q: How do traffic lights often detect that a car is waiting in front of them?
a: With an induction loop in the road
With a microphone on the post
With scales under the road surface
113282.e: In the road surface there is a wire loop with an alternating field. The metal of the car changes this field, and the system registers the vehicle.
113282.m: Induction loops in the road detect waiting cars.

113283.q: A transformer lowers 230 volts to 23 volts. What is the ratio of turns of the primary coil to the secondary coil?
113283.e: The voltage falls to a tenth, because 230 divided by 23 makes 10. So the primary coil has ten times as many turns as the secondary coil.
113283.m: A tenth of the voltage needs a tenth of the turns.

113284.q: What is the three-phase alternating current called that cookers and large machines run on?
113284.e: Three-phase current consists of three alternating currents that are offset from each other. It is ideal for powerful motors and large appliances.
113284.m: Three-phase current consists of three alternating currents.

113382.q: Why must you never use a plugged-in hairdryer near a full bath?
a: Because bath water conducts electricity and there is a risk of electric shock
Because the hairdryer would get too loud
Because the water would boil immediately
Because the hairdryer would then use less electricity
113382.e: Tap water contains dissolved substances and conducts electricity. If the hairdryer falls into the water, current can flow through the body, which can kill.
113382.m: Electrical appliances must be kept away from bath water.

113383.q: What happens to a lamp in a circuit when you open the switch?
113383.e: An open switch breaks the circuit. Without a closed path no current can flow, and the lamp goes out.
113383.m: An open switch breaks the circuit.

113384.e: Salt water contains dissolved salt particles that can carry electric charge. Pure, distilled water, on the other hand, conducts very poorly.
113384.m: Dissolved salt makes water a good conductor.

113385.q: Why is a cable covered in plastic on the outside?
a: To protect against electric shocks and short circuits
So that the current flows faster
So that the cable produces more voltage
113385.e: Plastic conducts practically no electricity. The covering protects people from touching the wire and stops bare conductors touching each other.
113385.m: The plastic covering of a cable protects against electric shocks.

113386.q: Why can a cable get very hot in a short circuit?
a: Because a very large current flows
Because no current flows at all
113386.e: In a short circuit the device with its resistance is missing. So a very large current flows, which heats the wire strongly.
113386.m: A short circuit produces a dangerously large current.

113387.q: What is a device in a circuit called that turns electrical energy into another form of energy, for example a lamp?
113387.e: Lamps, motors or heaters are called loads. They turn electrical energy into light, movement or heat.

113388.q: Which component supplies the electrical energy in a simple circuit?
113388.e: The battery is the voltage source. It drives the current and supplies the energy that the lamp turns into light.
113388.m: The battery is the source in the circuit.

113389.q: What is the direction of the so-called conventional current outside the source?
a: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal
From the negative terminal to the positive terminal
Always in a circle around the source
From the device back to the socket
113389.e: It was agreed long ago that current flows from plus to minus. In reality the electrons move the other way, but the rule is still used.
113389.m: Conventional current points from plus to minus.

113390.q: Why does a lamp not light up if you connect both wires only to the positive terminal of a battery?
a: The circuit is not closed across both terminals
113390.e: Current only flows if there is a path from one terminal to the other. Between two connections on the same terminal there is no voltage.
113390.m: A lamp needs a connection to both terminals of the source.

113391.q: How are two lamps connected in a series circuit?
a: One after the other on a single current path
With no connection to the source
113391.e: In a series circuit the current flows through all the devices one after the other. There is no branching.
113391.m: In a series circuit all devices are on one single path.

113392.q: How is a light switch connected to the lamp it switches on and off?
113392.e: The switch must be able to break the lamp's current path. So it is on the same path as the lamp, in other words in series.
113392.m: A switch is in series with the device it switches.

113393.q: How big is the current at different points in a series circuit?
113393.e: There is only one current path, and no charge is lost. So the same current flows through every component.
113393.m: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere.

113394.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to 12 V. What voltage is across each lamp?
113394.e: In a series circuit the total voltage is shared. With two identical lamps, each gets half: 12 V ÷ 2 = 6 V.
113394.m: In a series circuit the voltage is shared between the devices.

113395.q: In a series circuit there are 2 V, 3 V and 4 V across three components. What is the voltage of the source?
113395.e: In a series circuit the individual voltages add up to the total voltage: 2 V + 3 V + 4 V = 9 V.
113395.m: The individual voltages in a series circuit add up to the total voltage.

113396.q: How does the brightness change if you add a second identical lamp in series to a lamp?
a: Both shine more weakly than the one did before
Both shine as brightly as the one did before
113396.e: The total resistance gets bigger, and each lamp only gets half the voltage. So less current flows and both shine more weakly.
113396.m: More lamps in series shine more weakly.

113397.q: How do you connect three 1.5 V batteries to get a voltage of 4.5 V?
a: Only two of them in parallel
113397.e: When batteries are connected in series, their voltages add up: 1.5 V + 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 4.5 V.
113397.m: Batteries in series add their voltages.

113398.q: Two resistors of 10 ohms and 20 ohms are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
113398.e: In a series circuit the resistances add up: 10 ohms + 20 ohms = 30 ohms.

113399.q: What happens in a series circuit with two lamps if one lamp blows?
a: The other lamp shines more brightly
The other lamp keeps shining just as brightly
The battery goes flat at once
113399.e: In a series circuit there is only one current path. If one lamp is broken, no current can flow anywhere.
113399.m: In a series circuit one faulty device breaks the whole circuit.

113400.q: How are the lamps connected in a parallel circuit?
a: Each lamp on its own branch to the same source
All one after the other on one path
Only one lamp to the source
Without a switch and without a source
113400.e: In a parallel circuit the circuit branches. Each lamp is connected separately to both terminals of the source.
113400.m: In a parallel circuit each device has its own branch.

113401.q: What happens in a parallel circuit with two lamps if one lamp blows?
113401.e: Each branch is closed on its own. If one branch fails, current still flows in the other branch.
113401.m: In a parallel circuit the devices work independently of each other.

113402.q: How brightly do two identical lamps in parallel on a battery shine compared with a single lamp on the same battery?
113402.e: In a parallel circuit each lamp gets the full voltage of the battery. So the same current flows through each as through a single lamp.
113402.m: Lamps in parallel shine as brightly as when connected on their own.

113403.q: How are the sockets and lamps in a flat connected to the mains?
a: Alternately in series and in parallel
Not connected to each other at all
113403.e: Every device should get the full mains voltage and be able to be switched on and off by itself. That is only possible with a parallel circuit.
113403.m: Household devices are connected to the mains in parallel.

113404.q: In a parallel circuit, 0.2 A flows through one lamp and 0.3 A through the other. What is the total current?
113404.e: In a parallel circuit the branch currents add up to the total current: 0.2 A + 0.3 A = 0.5 A.
113404.m: In a parallel circuit the branch currents add up to the total current.

113405.q: 1.2 A flows through the main line of a parallel circuit. 0.5 A flows through one branch. What is the current in the second branch?
113405.e: The total current divides between the branches. That leaves 1.2 A minus 0.5 A, which is 0.7 A, for the second branch.
113405.m: In a parallel circuit the total current divides between the branches.

113406.q: What is the point called where a circuit splits into several branches?
113406.e: At a junction three or more wires meet. There the current divides or flows back together.
113406.m: At a junction the current branches.

113407.q: How does the total current from the battery change if you add another lamp in parallel?
113407.e: Each extra lamp opens another path for the current. The total current is the sum of all the branch currents and so gets bigger.
113407.m: Each new parallel branch increases the total current.

113408.q: Which device has a circle with a cross inside as its circuit symbol?
113408.e: In circuit diagrams a filament lamp is drawn as a circle with a diagonal cross. The cross is a reminder of the filament.
113408.m: A circle with a cross stands for a lamp.

113409.q: In the circuit symbol for a battery, what does the longer of the two lines mean?
113409.e: A battery cell is drawn with one long and one short line. The long line is the positive terminal, the short one the negative terminal.
113409.m: In the battery symbol the long line stands for plus.

113410.q: Which component is shown as a small rectangle according to the European standard?
113410.e: In Europe a resistor is drawn as a long rectangle. In American diagrams a zigzag line is drawn instead.
113410.m: A rectangle in a circuit diagram stands for a resistor.

113411.q: Which device has a circle with a large M inside as its circuit symbol?
113411.e: In circuit diagrams the letter M stands for motor. An electric motor turns electrical energy into movement.
113411.m: A circle with M stands for an electric motor.

113412.q: How is an open switch drawn in a circuit diagram?
a: As a line sticking out at an angle, with a gap
As a circle with a cross
113412.e: An open switch is drawn like a raised drawbridge. The gap shows that the circuit is broken.
113412.m: An open switch has a gap in its symbol.

113413.q: Which component is drawn as a triangle with a line across its tip and two small arrows pointing outwards?
113413.e: The triangle with a line is the symbol for a diode. The two arrows pointing outwards show that the diode gives off light, so it is an LED.
113413.m: An LED is drawn as a diode with light arrows.

113414.q: Why are circuit symbols used instead of pictures of the real components?
a: They are simple, clear and understood everywhere
Their colours are set by law
They show the exact size of the components
113414.e: Circuit symbols are standardised and reduced to the essentials. This lets experts all over the world read circuit diagrams quickly.
113414.m: Standard circuit symbols make diagrams clear.

113415.q: How is a point where two wires are connected shown in a circuit diagram?
113415.e: A thick dot at a crossing means the wires are connected. If lines cross without a dot, they are not connected.
113415.m: A dot in a circuit diagram shows that wires are connected.

a: A drawing of a circuit with standard symbols
A list of all the sockets in the house
113416.e: A circuit diagram uses symbols and lines to show how the components of a circuit are connected.
113416.m: A circuit diagram shows a circuit with symbols.

113417.q: How are the wires usually drawn in a circuit diagram?
a: As straight lines with right angles
113417.e: Wires are drawn horizontally and vertically wherever possible. This keeps the diagram clear, even if the real cables are not straight.
113417.m: In a circuit diagram wires are drawn straight and at right angles.

113418.q: What does a circuit diagram not show?
a: The exact position and length of the cables
Whether components are in series or in parallel
113418.e: A circuit diagram only shows the electrical connections. Where the cables actually run and how long they are cannot be seen from it.
113418.m: A circuit diagram shows connections, not the real position of the components.

113419.q: In a circuit diagram, a battery, a switch and two lamps are on a single closed line with no branches. Which circuit is this?
113419.e: Without branches, the current flows through all the components one after the other. That is the sign of a series circuit.
113419.m: A circuit without branches is a series circuit.

113420.q: How can you recognise a parallel circuit in a circuit diagram?
a: By the wire branching into several branches
113420.e: In a parallel circuit the wire splits into several paths at junctions. Each path has its own component.
113420.m: Branches in a circuit diagram show a parallel circuit.

113421.q: In a circuit diagram, a switch is in the main line before a branch to two lamps. What does it do?
a: It only switches the first lamp
It only switches the second lamp
113421.e: All the current flows through the main line. If you open the switch there, both branches are broken.
113421.m: A switch in the main line switches all the branches.

113422.q: What happens if you bridge a lamp in a circuit diagram directly with a wire?
a: The lamp is short-circuited and does not light
The lamp shines just as brightly
113422.e: The current takes the path with the least resistance through the bridge. Practically no current then flows through the lamp.

113423.q: Which circuit does a diagram show in which the stairwell light can be switched from two places?
113423.e: With two two-way switches you can switch a lamp on and off from two places. This circuit is called two-way switching and is common in stairwells.
113423.m: With two-way switching you switch a lamp from two places.

113424.q: What does electrical voltage tell you?
a: How strong the push driving the current is
How many cables are in the circuit
113424.e: Voltage is the push that moves the charges through the circuit. The bigger the voltage, the more strongly they are pushed.

113425.q: Which symbol is used for electrical voltage in German formulas?
113425.e: In German formulas U stands for voltage (in English, V is also common). Its unit is the volt.
113425.m: The formula symbol for voltage is U.

113426.q: In Switzerland, cookers are often connected to a high-power (three-phase) supply. What voltage does it have?
113426.e: Normal sockets have 230 V. Powerful appliances such as cookers use the three-phase supply with 400 V.
113426.m: The household three-phase supply has 400 volts.

113427.q: What does a battery supply: direct voltage or alternating voltage?
113427.e: With a battery, the positive and negative terminals always stay the same. So the current always flows in the same direction.

113428.q: What is the device called that turns the mains voltage into a small, adjustable voltage for experiments at school?
113428.e: A power supply unit is plugged into the socket and gives a safe low voltage. This can often be adjusted smoothly.
113428.m: A power supply unit gives small voltages for experiments.

113429.q: Why is mains voltage dangerous for people, but a 1.5 V battery is not?
a: The high voltage can drive a dangerously large current through the body
The body only conducts with batteries
113429.e: The bigger the voltage, the more current can flow through the body. At mains voltage the current can endanger the heart; at 1.5 V it is far too small.

113430.q: Where in a circuit is there a voltage even when the switch is open?
a: Between the terminals of the battery
113430.e: A battery always has a voltage across its terminals, even when no current flows. But current only flows once the circuit is closed.
113430.m: A voltage can be there even when no current flows.

113431.q: At what voltage do most SBB trains run via the overhead line?
113431.e: The SBB's overhead lines carry an alternating voltage of 15,000 volts, which is 15 kilovolts. The locomotive converts it for its motors.

113432.q: Which country did Alessandro Volta, after whom the unit volt is named, come from?
113432.e: Alessandro Volta was born in Como in 1745 and taught at the University of Pavia. He was one of the most important pioneers of electricity.
113432.m: Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist.

113433.q: What is the first battery that Alessandro Volta built around 1800 called?
113433.e: Volta stacked metal discs and cardboard soaked in salt water on top of each other in turn. This pile was the first to supply a lasting electric current.
113433.m: The voltaic pile was the first battery.

113434.q: Which metals were the discs of a voltaic pile typically made of?
113434.e: Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper, sometimes silver, with damp cardboard in between. A voltage forms between the different metals.
113434.m: Two different metals in salt water produce a voltage.

113435.q: How many volts are there in 1 kilovolt?
113435.e: The prefix kilo means thousand. So 1 kV = 1000 V.
113435.m: One kilovolt is a thousand volts.

113436.m: One volt is a thousand millivolts.

113437.q: What voltage does the starter battery of an ordinary car have?
113437.e: Most cars have a 12-volt battery. It supplies the current for the starter motor and the on-board electronics.

113438.q: Roughly what voltage does a single lithium-ion cell, like the ones in mobile phones, have?
113438.e: A lithium-ion cell has a nominal voltage of about 3.6 to 3.7 volts. That is much more than an ordinary battery cell.
113438.m: A lithium-ion cell has around 3.7 volts.

113440.q: What does electric current tell you?
a: How much charge flows through a conductor per second
113440.e: Current tells you how much electric charge flows through a cross-section of the conductor every second.
113440.m: Current measures how much charge flows per second.

113441.q: Which formula symbol is used for current?
113441.e: Current has the formula symbol I. It comes from the French word “intensité”.
113441.m: The formula symbol for current is I.

113442.q: Which formula do you use to work out current from voltage and resistance?
113442.e: According to Ohm's law, U = R × I. Rearranging for I gives I = U / R.
113442.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

113443.q: How does the current change if, with the same voltage, you use a resistance twice as big?
113443.e: According to I = U / R, the current gets smaller when the resistance gets bigger. With double the resistance, only half as much current flows.
113443.m: Double the resistance means half the current at the same voltage.

113444.q: What happens to the current through a lamp if you increase the voltage?
113444.e: A bigger voltage pushes the current harder. So more current flows and the lamp shines more brightly.

113445.q: At what current is an ordinary small LED typically run?
113445.e: Small standard LEDs are usually designed for about 20 milliamps. A series resistor makes sure the current doesn't get too big.
113445.m: Small LEDs only need a few milliamps.

113446.q: Which effect of electric current does a kettle use?
113446.e: When current flows through the heating element, it gets hot. The heat is passed on to the water.
113446.m: A kettle uses the heating effect of current.

113447.q: Which effect of electric current is used to copper-plate or gold-plate objects?
113447.e: When current flows through a metal salt solution, metal is deposited on the object. This process is called electroplating.
113447.m: Electroplating uses the chemical effect of current.

113448.q: Which effect of electric current does an electromagnet use?
113448.e: Every conductor carrying a current produces a magnetic field. In a coil with an iron core it becomes so strong that it attracts iron.

113449.q: Who is the unit ampere named after?
113449.e: In the 19th century the physicist André-Marie Ampère studied the magnetic effect of current. In his honour the unit of current is called the ampere.
113449.m: The unit ampere honours André-Marie Ampère.

113450.q: Which country did André-Marie Ampère come from?
113450.e: Ampère was born in Lyon in 1775 and worked in Paris. He is seen as one of the founders of electrodynamics.
113450.m: André-Marie Ampère was a French physicist.

113451.q: How many milliamps are there in 1 amp?
113451.e: The prefix milli means one thousandth. So 1 A = 1000 mA.
113451.m: One amp is a thousand milliamps.

113452.m: Divide milliamps by a thousand to get amps.

113453.q: Which abbreviation stands for the unit ampere?
113453.e: The unit ampere is abbreviated with the capital letter A. Instruments for measuring current also carry this symbol.
113453.m: The abbreviation for ampere is A.

113454.q: What is true of the ampere in the International System of Units (SI)?
a: It is one of the seven base units
It is not an official unit
It is a unit of voltage
It is a unit of energy
113454.e: The SI has seven base units, including the metre, kilogram, second and ampere. The volt, on the other hand, is a derived unit.
113454.m: The ampere is an SI base unit.

113455.q: Roughly what current is typical in a lightning strike?
113455.e: In a lightning strike, typically tens of thousands of amps flow for a very short time. That is why lightning is so dangerous.
113455.m: Huge currents flow in a lightning strike.

113456.q: What current is already dangerous for a person if it flows through the body?
113456.e: Even currents of a few dozen milliamps can upset the rhythm of the heart. That is why safety switches in homes are set to be very sensitive.
113456.m: Even small currents through the body can kill.

113457.q: What is the minimum number of ammeters you need to measure both branch currents at the same time in a parallel circuit with two lamps?
113457.e: Each branch has its own current. To measure both at the same time, each branch needs its own ammeter.
113457.m: Each branch current needs its own ammeter.

113458.q: How is an ammeter placed in a circuit?
a: With no connection to the circuit
113458.e: All the current you want to measure must flow through the ammeter. So it is inserted into the circuit, in other words connected in series.
113458.m: An ammeter is connected in series.

113459.q: Why does an ammeter have a very small internal resistance?
a: So that it hardly changes the current in the circuit
So that it produces more voltage
113459.e: The ammeter sits in the current path. If it had a large resistance, it would slow the current and give a false reading.
113459.m: A good ammeter has a very small resistance.

113460.q: What can happen if you connect an ammeter directly to the terminals of a battery?
a: A short circuit that can damage the meter
113460.e: Because of its small resistance, a very large current then flows. The fuse in the meter can blow or the meter gets damaged.
113460.m: An ammeter must never be connected directly to the source.

113461.q: What does the circuit symbol for an ammeter look like?
a: A circle with an A inside
A circle with a V inside
A rectangle with an A inside
A triangle with an A inside
113461.e: Meters are drawn as circles. The letter A shows that amps, in other words current, are being measured.
113461.m: An ammeter is drawn as a circle with an A.

113462.q: An ammeter is set to the 1 A range. The pointer is exactly in the middle of the scale. What current is flowing?
113462.e: Full deflection at the end of the scale matches the 1 A range. The middle of the scale means half of that: 1 A ÷ 2 = 0.5 A.
113462.m: When reading a meter, always note the range it is set to.

113463.q: Where must you place the ammeter to measure the total current of a parallel circuit?
a: In the main line before the branch
113463.e: The current of all the branches flows together through the main line. So an ammeter there measures the total current.
113463.m: You measure the total current in the main line.

113464.q: What does an ammeter show when the switch in the circuit is open?
113464.e: With the switch open, the circuit is broken. No current flows, so the ammeter shows zero.
113464.m: Without a closed circuit the ammeter shows zero.

113465.e: A voltmeter shows what voltage there is between two points in a circuit. The reading is in volts.

113466.q: How is a voltmeter connected to measure the voltage across a lamp?
a: Only to one terminal of the lamp
In series between the lamp and the switch
113466.e: Voltage exists between two points. So you connect the voltmeter to both terminals of the lamp, in other words in parallel.
113466.m: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.

113467.q: Why does a voltmeter have a very large internal resistance?
a: So that hardly any current flows through the meter
So that it doubles the voltage
113467.e: The voltmeter sits in parallel with the component. Because of the large resistance almost no current flows through it, and the circuit is hardly affected.
113467.m: A good voltmeter has a very large resistance.

113468.q: What does the circuit symbol for a voltmeter look like?
a: A circle with a V inside
A circle with an A inside
A circle with a cross inside
A rectangle with a V inside
113468.e: Meters are drawn as circles. The V shows that voltage is measured in volts.
113468.m: A voltmeter is drawn as a circle with a V.

113469.q: A voltmeter is held against the terminals of a new flat 4.5 V battery. Roughly what reading does it show?
113469.e: A new flat battery has a nominal voltage of 4.5 V. The voltmeter shows roughly this value.

113470.q: What does a voltmeter show when connected across a closed switch in a circuit?
113470.e: A closed switch is a good conductor with almost no resistance. So practically no voltage is dropped across its terminals.
113470.m: There is almost no voltage across a closed switch.

113471.q: What does a voltmeter show across an open switch in a simple circuit with a battery and a lamp?
113471.e: With the switch open no current flows, and no voltage is dropped across the lamp. So the whole battery voltage is across the gap in the switch.
113471.m: The whole voltage of the source is across an open switch.

113472.q: What happens if you wrongly connect a voltmeter in series with the lamp?
a: The lamp hardly lights because almost no current flows
113472.e: The large internal resistance of the voltmeter lets almost no current through. The lamp stays dark, and the voltmeter shows roughly the battery voltage.
113472.m: A voltmeter in series blocks the current almost completely.

a: A meter for several electrical quantities
A device that only measures time
113473.e: Depending on the setting, a multimeter can measure voltage, current and resistance. That is why it has its name.
113473.m: A multimeter measures different electrical quantities.

113474.q: Which socket of a multimeter is the black test lead usually connected to?
113474.e: COM stands for “common”, the shared reference socket. The black lead stays there for almost all measurements; the red one is moved depending on the measurement.
113474.m: The black test lead goes in the COM socket.

113475.q: What does a multimeter measure on the setting A with a straight line next to it?
113475.e: The A stands for amps, in other words current. The straight line means direct current, like that from a battery.
113475.m: A with a straight line means direct current.

113476.q: Why do you only measure a resistance with a multimeter when the circuit is switched off?
a: Because the meter itself produces a small measuring current
Because resistances can only be measured at night
Because the resistance would otherwise disappear
Because the display would otherwise be too bright
113476.e: To measure resistance, the multimeter sends its own small current through the component. Other voltages would give a false reading or damage the meter.
113476.m: Resistances are only measured in circuits with no power.

113477.q: Which range do you choose on a multimeter if you don't know how big the voltage is?
113477.e: If you start with the largest range, the meter cannot be overloaded. Then you switch step by step to smaller ranges for more precise values.
113477.m: With unknown values, start with the largest range.

113478.q: What does a wavy line (~) next to the V on a multimeter show?
113478.e: The wavy line stands for alternating voltage, like that from a socket. Straight lines, on the other hand, mark direct voltage.
113478.m: A wavy line means alternating voltage.

113479.q: What does a minus sign in front of the reading mean when measuring direct voltage with a multimeter?
a: The test leads are connected the wrong way round
113479.e: The multimeter also shows the direction of the voltage. If you hold the red lead to minus and the black one to plus, a minus sign appears.
113479.m: A minus sign shows the test leads are swapped.

113480.q: What is the continuity test on a multimeter, where the meter beeps, used for?
a: To check whether a wire is connected all the way through
113480.e: In the continuity test, the meter beeps if there is a very small resistance between the probes. This lets you quickly find broken cables.
113480.m: With the continuity test you find broken wires.

113481.q: Which socket of a multimeter do you plug the red lead into to measure large currents of a few amps?
113481.e: For large currents a multimeter has its own specially protected socket, usually labelled 10A. The mA socket is only meant for small currents.
113481.m: Large currents are measured through the 10A socket.

113573.q: A 9-volt battery drives a current of 0.5 amps through a small bulb. What is the resistance?
113573.e: Resistance is voltage divided by current. 9 V / 0.5 A makes 18 Ω.
113573.m: You get resistance from voltage divided by current.

113574.q: 2 amps flow through a resistance of 6 ohms. What voltage is applied?
113574.e: Voltage is resistance times current. 6 Ω × 2 A makes 12 V.
113574.m: You get voltage from resistance times current.

113575.q: What does the graph of current against voltage look like for an ohmic resistor?
a: A straight line through the origin
113575.e: Because current and voltage are proportional, all the measured points lie on a straight line. It starts at the origin, because without voltage no current flows.
113575.m: For an ohmic resistor, the measurements give a straight line through the origin.

113576.q: Suppose a human body has a resistance of 1000 ohms. How big would the current be at 230 volts?
113576.e: 230 V / 1000 Ω makes 0.23 A, which is 230 milliamps. Even much smaller currents can kill a person.
113576.m: Even the voltage from a socket can drive a deadly current through the body.

113577.q: A 4.5-volt flat battery is connected to a resistance of 15 ohms. How big is the current?
113577.e: You work out 4.5 V / 15 Ω. That makes 0.3 A.
113577.m: With Ohm's law you can work out any of the three quantities.

113578.q: A small bulb with a resistance of 12 ohms is connected to a voltage of 6 volts. How big is the current?
113578.e: You divide the voltage by the resistance. 6 V / 12 Ω makes 0.5 A.
113578.m: If the resistance in ohms is bigger than the voltage in volts, less than one amp flows.

113579.q: What resistance is needed for exactly 2 amps to flow at 230 volts?
113579.e: Resistance is voltage divided by current. 230 V / 2 A makes 115 Ω.
113579.m: With Ohm's law you can work out the right resistance.

113580.q: What happens to the current if you halve the resistance at the same voltage?
113580.e: According to Ohm's law, current is voltage divided by resistance. If the number you divide by becomes half as big, the result becomes twice as big.
113580.m: A smaller resistance lets more current flow at the same voltage.

113581.q: Which formula symbol is used for electrical resistance?
113581.e: The R comes from the Latin word resistere, which means to resist. U stands for voltage and I for current.
113581.m: Electrical resistance has the formula symbol R.

113582.q: How does the resistance change if you use a thicker wire made of the same metal?
113582.e: A thicker wire offers the current a larger cross-section. So its resistance falls.
113582.m: The thicker a wire, the smaller its resistance.

113583.q: What usually happens to the resistance of a metal wire when it gets hot?
113583.e: In a hot metal the atoms vibrate more strongly. The electrons are slowed down more often, and the resistance rises.
113583.m: In metals, resistance rises with temperature.

113584.q: What are materials called whose resistance disappears completely at very low temperatures?
113584.e: Below a certain very low temperature, superconductors conduct electricity with no resistance at all. They are used, for example, for strong magnets in hospitals and particle accelerators.
113584.m: Superconductors have no resistance at very low temperatures.

113585.q: What is the resistance of the heating element in a kettle for?
113585.e: When current flows through a resistance, electrical energy is turned into heat. The heating element gets hot and warms the water.
113585.m: A heating element uses resistance to produce heat.

113586.q: Two resistors of 100 ohms each are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
113586.e: In a parallel circuit the current has two paths and gets through more easily. Two equal resistors together give half, so 100 Ω / 2 equals 50 Ω.
113586.m: Resistors in parallel give a smaller total resistance.

113587.q: What is a component called whose resistance you can adjust with a knob?
113587.e: A potentiometer is an adjustable resistor. It is found, for example, in old volume controls or dimmers.
113587.m: With a potentiometer you can adjust the resistance.

113588.q: Which Greek letter is the symbol for the unit ohm?
113588.e: The ohm is abbreviated with the capital Greek omega, which looks like this: Ω. This way it is not confused with the digit 0.
113588.m: The symbol for ohm is the Greek omega.

113589.q: What did Georg Simon Ohm, after whom the unit ohm is named, study?
a: How voltage and current are related
How light is refracted in glass
113589.e: Ohm found that in a wire the current grows in the same proportion as the voltage. He published this in 1827; today it is called Ohm's law.
113589.m: The unit ohm honours the physicist Georg Simon Ohm.

113590.q: Which quantity is measured in ohms?
113590.e: Resistance tells you how strongly a component holds back the current. Voltage is measured in volts, current in amps and power in watts.
113590.m: Electrical resistance is measured in ohms.

113591.q: What resistance does a component have if exactly 1 amp flows through it at 1 volt?
113591.e: One ohm is defined as one volt per amp. 1 V / 1 A makes exactly 1 Ω.
113591.m: One ohm equals one volt per amp.

113592.m: One kilohm is a thousand ohms.

113593.e: Mega means a million. 2 × 1,000,000 makes 2,000,000 Ω.
113593.m: One megohm is a million ohms.

113594.q: Which instrument can you use to measure a resistance in ohms?
113594.e: A multimeter can measure voltage, current and resistance. To measure resistance you set it to the ohm range.
113594.m: Resistances are measured with a multimeter.

113595.q: What do the coloured rings on small resistors in electronics show?
113595.e: Each colour stands for a digit or a multiplier. This lets you read the value even on tiny components.
113595.m: The colour rings reveal the value of a resistor.

113597.q: Why do metals conduct electricity well?
113597.e: In metals some electrons are not tightly bound to an atom. These free electrons can move and so carry the current.
113597.m: Free electrons make metals good conductors.

113598.q: What is the insulation around the wires of an electric cable usually made of?
113598.e: Plastic is an insulator and lets almost no current through. The covering protects against touching the live wires.
113598.m: Plastic insulates the wires in cables.

113600.q: Why does ordinary tap water conduct electricity?
a: Because salts are dissolved in it
Because it comes from the mountains
113600.e: Tap water contains dissolved mineral salts that form charged particles. That is why water and electrical appliances are dangerous together.

113601.q: Which substance in a pencil lead conducts electricity?
113601.e: Pencil leads are made of graphite and clay; they contain no lead. Graphite is a form of carbon that conducts electricity.
113601.m: Graphite in pencil leads is an electrical conductor.

113602.e: Silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals, just ahead of copper. Because it is expensive, it is only rarely used for cables.
113602.m: Silver is the best metallic conductor.

113604.q: Is dry air normally an electrical conductor or an insulator?
113604.e: Dry air normally lets hardly any current through. Only at very high voltage, as with lightning, can a current pass through the air.
113604.m: Air insulates as long as the voltage is not extremely high.

113605.q: Why is a short circuit dangerous?
a: The wires heat up strongly and can catch fire
The voltage falls to zero and everything gets cold
113605.e: Because of the very large current, the wires get hot. Without protection the insulation can melt and a fire can start.
113605.m: The great heat of a short circuit can start a fire.

113606.q: What is a common cause of a short circuit?
a: A lamp that is too bright
113606.e: If a cable's insulation is damaged, the wires can touch. Then the current flows directly from one conductor to the other.
113606.m: Damaged cables are a common cause of short circuits.

113607.q: How big is the resistance of the circuit in a short circuit?
113607.e: In a short circuit the resistance of the device is missing; only the small resistance of the wires remains. According to Ohm's law the current then becomes huge.
113607.m: In a short circuit the resistance is very small and the current very large.

113608.q: In a short circuit at 230 volts the resistance is only 0.5 ohms. What current would flow?
113608.e: You work out 230 V / 0.5 Ω. That makes 460 A, many times the normal current in a household wire.
113608.m: A tiny resistance leads to a huge short-circuit current.

113609.q: What can be seen at the fault point in a short circuit?
113609.e: The large current can heat the air at the fault point so much that it glows. This produces sparks or a bright electric arc.
113609.m: A short circuit can produce sparks and electric arcs.

113610.q: Which device in the house automatically cuts off the current in a short circuit?
113610.e: The fuse detects the excessive current and breaks the circuit. This prevents a fire.
113610.m: In a short circuit the fuse trips.

113611.q: Why should you not carry loose batteries in your pocket together with keys or coins?
a: The metal can short-circuit the terminals
113611.e: If a piece of metal touches both terminals at once, a short circuit occurs. The battery can get hot and in the worst case catch fire.
113611.m: Metal in your pocket can short-circuit a battery.

113612.q: When a standard lamp is switched on, the fuse trips immediately. What is the most likely cause?
a: A short circuit in the lamp
A bulb that is too weak
Too little voltage in the mains
113612.e: If the fuse trips exactly when a device is switched on, a very large current is suddenly flowing there. Usually a short circuit in the device or cable is to blame, and it should be checked.
113612.m: If the fuse trips when you switch on, a short circuit in the device is often to blame.

113613.q: How does a cartridge fuse work?
a: A thin wire melts if the current is too high
A magnet pulls out the plug
113613.e: A cartridge fuse contains a thin fuse wire. If the current gets too big, it gets so hot that it melts and breaks the circuit.
113613.m: In a cartridge fuse a thin wire melts if there is too much current.

113614.q: What must you do after a cartridge fuse has blown?
a: Replace it with a new one
113614.e: The fuse wire is destroyed when the fuse blows. So the fuse must be replaced with a new one of the same rating.
113614.m: A blown cartridge fuse must be replaced.

113615.q: What does a fuse in the house mainly protect against?
a: Electricity bills that are too high
113615.e: The fuse switches off if too much current flows through a wire. This stops the cables getting too hot and prevents a fire.
113615.m: Fuses protect the wires from overheating.

113616.q: What is the advantage of a circuit breaker over a cartridge fuse?
a: You can switch it back on
It lets much more current through
113616.e: A circuit breaker switches off when there is too much current. Once the fault has been fixed, you simply flip the lever back.
113616.m: A circuit breaker can be switched back on after it trips.

113617.q: In which unit is the rating on a fuse given?
113617.e: A fuse shows the current at which it still does not trip over time, for example 10 A. If much more current flows, it switches off.
113617.m: Fuses are rated by current in amps.

113618.q: Why must you never bridge a blown fuse with a piece of wire?
a: Because there would then be no protection against overheating
Because the wire conducts too little current
Because the fuse would otherwise cost more
113618.e: A thick wire does not melt when the current is too high. The wires can then overheat and cause a fire.
113618.m: A fuse must never be bridged with wire.

113619.q: What can happen if you fit a fuse with too high an amp rating?
a: The wires can overheat before it trips
113619.e: A fuse that is too big lets through more current than the wire can take. The cables can get hot and cause a fire before the fuse switches off.
113619.m: A fuse must match the wire.

113620.q: Where are the fuses in a house?
113620.e: In the fuse box, also called the consumer unit, each circuit has its own fuse. There you can switch off individual parts of the home.
113620.m: A house's fuses are in the fuse box.

113621.q: What does a residual current device constantly compare?
a: The current flowing out with the current flowing back
The voltage with the time of day
The electricity price with the usage
113621.e: Normally the same amount of current flows to the device as flows back. If some is missing, it is flowing away somewhere else, and the device trips.
113621.m: An RCD notices when current takes a wrong path.

113622.q: At what fault current does an RCD for protecting people typically trip?
113622.e: RCDs for protecting people trip at a fault current of 30 milliamps at the latest. That is much less than an ordinary fuse needs.
113622.m: To protect people, an RCD trips at 30 milliamps.

113623.e: Milli means one thousandth. 30 divided by 1000 makes 0.03 A.
113623.m: One milliamp is a thousandth of an amp.

113624.q: How quickly does an RCD switch off when there is a fault?
a: In a fraction of a second
113624.e: An RCD cuts the circuit within fractions of a second. This keeps the time in which current flows through a body very short.
113624.m: An RCD switches off in a flash.

113625.q: What should you do with the test button of an RCD?
a: Press it regularly to test that it works
Keep it pressed all the time
113625.e: Pressing the test button imitates a fault current. If the RCD switches off, it is working properly.
113625.m: The test button shows whether the RCD still works.

a: Current that flows to earth by a wrong path
Current that stands still in the cable
113626.e: A fault current does not flow back through the intended wire, but, for example, through a casing or a person into the earth. That is exactly what the safety switch detects.
113626.m: A fault current takes a wrong path, often through the earth.

113627.q: What is the residual current device often called for short in Switzerland?
113627.e: F stands for Fehlerstrom (fault current) and I for the formula symbol of current. An LS switch, on the other hand, is a circuit breaker. In English it is usually called an RCD.
113627.m: In Switzerland the RCD is called an FI switch for short.

113628.q: Where is an RCD especially important because the risk of electric shock is higher there?
a: In the bedroom and the attic
In the stairwell and the cellar
In the office and the living room
113628.e: Where there is water and damp, the body has a good connection to the earth. An RCD can save lives there in an accident.
113628.m: Where it is wet, an RCD protects especially well.

113629.q: What does earthing mean in electrical engineering?
a: A conducting connection to the ground
113629.e: In earthing, part of the installation is connected to the ground by a conductor. This lets current flow safely into the earth if there is a fault.
113629.m: Earthing connects an installation to the ground by a conductor.

113630.q: What is a lightning conductor on a house for?
a: It carries the lightning current safely into the earth
It draws thunderstorms away from the house
It stores the energy of the lightning
113630.e: If lightning strikes, the current flows through the rod and thick cables into the ground. So the house is not damaged.
113630.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning current into the earth.

113631.q: What is a foundation earth electrode?
a: A metal strip in the concrete foundation of a building
A cable in the roof space
113631.e: During construction a metal strip is laid in the foundation. Through the concrete it has good contact with the earth and serves as earthing for the whole house.
113631.m: The foundation earth electrode earths the whole building through its foundation.

113632.q: Why are the metal casings of many devices earthed?
a: So that fault current doesn't flow through people
So that the devices use less electricity
So that they warm up faster
113632.e: If a faulty wire touches the casing, the current flows away through the earth. This makes the protective device switch off before anyone gets an electric shock.
113632.m: Earthing carries dangerous currents past people.

113633.q: What does equipotential bonding in a house connect?
a: Metal parts such as water and heating pipes
The electricity bills of all the flats
113633.e: In equipotential bonding, conductive parts such as pipes are connected to each other and to the earthing. So there is no dangerous voltage between them.
113633.m: Equipotential bonding prevents voltages between metal parts.

113634.q: Why is it especially dangerous to touch a faulty device while barefoot on a wet floor?
a: Because the body is then well connected to the earth
Because the device then gives more light
113634.e: Wet skin and a wet floor have a small resistance. Current can then easily flow through the body into the earth.
113634.m: On a wet floor, current flows through the body especially easily.

113635.q: What voltage does the earth have as a reference point in electrical engineering?
113635.e: The earth counts as the reference point with 0 volts. All other voltages in an installation are given relative to this point.
113635.m: As a reference point, the earth has zero voltage.

113636.q: Why is a tanker lorry earthed while it is being filled with petrol?
a: So that no dangerous charge builds up
So that the petrol flows faster
So that the tank doesn't rust
113636.e: When fuel is transferred, electric charge can build up. A spark could ignite the petrol fumes, so the charge is carried away through the earthing.
113636.m: Earthing prevents dangerous sparks when transferring petrol.

113637.q: What colour is the protective earth wire in an electric cable?
113637.e: The protective earth wire has green and yellow stripes everywhere in the world. This colour must not be used for any other wire.
113637.m: The earth wire is always green and yellow.

113638.q: Which part of a device is the protective earth wire connected to?
113638.e: The protective earth wire connects the touchable metal casing to the earthing. If there is a fault, the current flows away through it.
113638.m: The earth wire is connected to the metal casing of a device.

113639.q: What colour is the neutral wire in a household installation?
113639.e: The neutral wire is blue. In normal use the current flows back from the device through it.

113640.q: What colour is the live wire, which carries the voltage, usually in an appliance cable?
113640.e: The live wire, often also called the phase, is usually brown in appliance cables. In installations, black and grey are also used.
113640.m: The live wire is usually brown.

113641.q: How many pins does a Swiss mains plug with a protective earth have?
113641.e: The Swiss plug with a protective earth has three pins. The middle pin, which is slightly offset, is connected to the earth wire.
113641.m: The Swiss plug with an earth has three pins.

113642.q: Why do double-insulated devices of protection class II not need an earth wire?
a: Because the live parts are covered twice
Because they are only used outdoors
Because they are always switched off
113642.e: These devices have extra insulation built in, for example a plastic casing. You can recognise them by the symbol of two squares, one inside the other.
113642.m: Double-insulated devices manage without an earth wire.

113643.q: What happens if, in a device with an earth wire, a live wire touches the metal casing?
a: The current flows away through the earth wire and the fuse trips
The device simply keeps running as usual
The voltage in the whole house rises
113643.e: Through the earth wire, a short circuit to earth with a large current occurs. This makes the protective device switch off the circuit.
113643.m: The earth wire makes sure the power is cut when there is a fault.

113644.q: What is the danger if the earth wire of a device with a metal casing is broken and a fault occurs?
a: The casing gets cold at once
113644.e: Without an earth wire the fault current cannot flow away. Anyone who touches the casing can then become the path for the current themselves.
113644.m: Without an earth wire, a faulty casing can be deadly.

113645.q: How many pins does an ordinary earthed Swiss plug have?
113645.e: The earthed Swiss plug has three round pins. They are for the live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire.
113645.m: An earthed Swiss plug has three pins.

113646.q: Why doesn't a German Schuko plug fit into a Swiss socket?
a: It is too wide and round
113646.e: The Schuko plug has a round body with earth contacts on the sides. It is too big for the narrow Swiss socket, so you need an adapter.
113646.m: In Switzerland you need an adapter for German Schuko plugs.

113647.q: What shape is the body of a Swiss type 12 plug?
113647.e: The Swiss plug has a flat, hexagonal body. This lets it fit exactly into the matching recess of the socket.
113647.m: The Swiss plug has a hexagonal shape.

113648.q: Which pin of the three-pin Swiss plug is the earth?
a: The middle pin, which is slightly offset
113648.e: The earth pin is in the middle and is slightly offset from the line of the other two pins. This means the plug can only be put in the right way round.
113648.m: On the Swiss plug the middle pin is the earth.

113649.q: What current are ordinary Swiss type 13 sockets designed for?
113649.e: Normal household sockets are built for at most 10 amps. For bigger currents there are sockets with square pins for 16 amps.
113649.m: Normal Swiss sockets are designed for 10 amps.

113650.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland also uses the type J plug system?
113650.e: Liechtenstein uses the same plugs and sockets as Switzerland. In the other neighbouring countries Schuko or French plugs are usual.
113650.m: Liechtenstein also uses Swiss type J plugs.

113651.q: What is the earth wire, in other words the middle pin of the Swiss plug, for?
a: It safely carries the current away if there is a fault
It just holds the plug in place
113651.e: If a wire inside the device touches the metal casing, the current flows away through the earth wire. The fuse trips, and you don't get an electric shock.
113651.m: The earth wire protects against electric shocks.

113652.q: How many pins does the Swiss type 11 plug have?
113652.e: Type 11 is a two-pin plug without an earth. It is used for double-insulated devices.
113652.m: The Swiss type 11 plug has only two pins.

113653.q: What kind of current does a household socket supply?
113653.e: With alternating current the current keeps changing direction. Batteries, on the other hand, supply direct current, which always flows the same way.

113654.q: What voltage does an ordinary socket in Switzerland supply?
113654.e: Swiss household sockets supply 230 volts alternating voltage. Large appliances such as cookers sometimes even use 400 volts.

113655.q: From what alternating voltage is touching generally considered dangerous?
113655.e: Alternating voltages up to 50 volts count as extra-low voltage; above that, touching is dangerous. The 230 volts from a socket are far above that.
113655.m: Alternating voltages above 50 volts can kill.

113656.q: A kettle has a power of 2300 watts and runs on 230 volts. What current flows?
113656.e: Power is voltage times current. So 2300 W / 230 V gives a current of 10 A.
113656.m: Current is power divided by voltage.

113657.q: What does a mobile phone charger do with the 230-volt mains voltage?
a: It converts it into a small direct voltage
It passes it unchanged into the phone
113657.e: The charger turns the mains voltage into a small direct voltage, usually 5 volts for USB. This lets the battery be charged safely.
113657.m: A charger turns 230 volts into a small direct voltage.

113658.q: What mains voltage is usual in homes in the USA?
113658.e: In North America sockets supply around 120 volts. Travellers therefore have to check whether their devices can handle both voltages.
113658.m: In the USA the mains voltage is lower than in Europe.

113659.q: A hairdryer has a power of 1150 watts and runs on 230 volts. What current flows?
113659.e: Current is power divided by voltage. 1150 W / 230 V makes 5 A.
113659.m: You can work out the current from power and voltage.

113660.q: What does “230 V” on a device's rating plate mean?
a: The device is built for a 230-volt mains supply
The device needs 230 watts of power
The device lasts 230 hours of use
113660.e: The rating plate gives the voltage a device is built for. A device for 230 volts suits the Swiss power grid.
113660.m: The rating plate says what voltage a device is built for.

113661.q: Why is even getting close to a railway overhead line deadly?
a: The current can jump across as an electric arc
The line pulls people in magnetically
113661.e: At very high voltage, the current can jump through the air without you touching the line. So you must always keep a long distance away.
113661.m: Never get close to an overhead line, even without touching it.

113662.q: Is an overhead line live when no train is running?
a: No, only when a train is coming
113662.e: Overhead lines are switched on all the time, even when no train can be seen. So you must always treat them as deadly.
113662.m: An overhead line is always live.

113663.q: Why must you never climb onto parked goods wagons?
a: Because you get too close to the overhead line
Because the wagons have just been painted
Because the wagons start moving at once
Because the roof is made of glass
113663.e: On the roof of a wagon you are only a short distance from the overhead line. Again and again young people are badly injured or killed by an electric shock doing this.
113663.m: Climbing on railway wagons is deadly because of the overhead line.

113664.q: Why doesn't a bird on a single power line get an electric shock?
a: Because there is hardly any voltage between its feet
Because its feathers store the electricity
Because the line carries no current
113664.e: Both feet are on the same line, so the voltage difference between them is tiny. It only becomes dangerous if it touches something at another potential at the same time, for example a pylon.
113664.m: Current only flows when there is a voltage difference.

113665.q: What is the part on the roof of a locomotive that collects current from the overhead line called?
113665.e: The pantograph presses a contact strip up against the contact wire from below. This is how the current gets into the locomotive.
113665.m: A pantograph collects current from the overhead line.

113666.q: By what route does the railway current flow back from the locomotive?
113666.e: The current flows through the wheels into the rails and from there back to the substation. So the rails are part of the circuit.
113666.m: On the railway, the rails serve as the return conductor.

113667.q: Where does a large part of the SBB's railway electricity come from?
a: From its own hydroelectric power stations
113667.e: The SBB runs its own hydroelectric power stations in the Alps. There it produces a large part of the electricity for its trains itself.
113667.m: The SBB produces much of its railway electricity with its own hydropower.

113668.q: Why should you never fly kites near railway or power lines?
a: The string can carry the current to a person
The kite is attracted by the electricity
The wind is too weak there
The line cuts through the string
113668.e: If the string touches a line or comes too close to it, current can flow through the string, especially if it is damp. That can be fatal.
113668.m: Keep kites far away from power lines.

113669.q: Is a tram's overhead line harmless because it has a lower voltage than the railway's?
a: Yes, but only in dry weather
113669.e: Trams do run on a lower voltage than trains, usually around 600 volts. But that is still far more than enough to kill a person.
113669.m: A tram's overhead line also carries a dangerously high voltage.

a: Natural substances from plants that are often poisonous
113866.e: Alkaloids are made mainly by plants. Many have a strong effect on the body, for example caffeine or nicotine.
113866.m: Alkaloids are strong, often poisonous plant substances.

113867.q: Which poisonous alkaloid forms in green patches on potatoes?
113867.e: Green patches and sprouts on potatoes contain solanine. That is why you cut them away generously before cooking.
113867.m: Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.

113868.q: Which well-known alkaloid is found in coffee beans?
113868.e: Caffeine is an alkaloid that keeps you awake. It is also found in tea leaves, for example.
113868.m: The caffeine in coffee is also an alkaloid.

113869.q: Which alkaloid comes from the tobacco plant?
113869.e: The tobacco plant makes nicotine in its leaves. For insects it is a strong poison.
113869.m: Nicotine is the poisonous alkaloid of the tobacco plant.

113870.q: What do most alkaloids taste like?
113870.e: Most alkaloids taste bitter. The bitter taste often warns animals and people of something poisonous.
113870.m: Many plant poisons taste bitter and so warn of danger.

113871.q: What are alkaloids probably for in the plant itself?
a: Protection from animals that eat them
113871.e: Plants cannot run away. Poisonous and bitter substances such as alkaloids stop many animals from eating them.
113871.m: Plants protect themselves with alkaloids from animals that want to eat them.

113872.q: Which plant is the alkaloid morphine obtained from?
113872.e: Morphine comes from the milky sap of the opium poppy. It is a strong painkiller that only doctors may prescribe.
113872.m: The painkiller morphine is obtained from the opium poppy.

113873.q: Why must you not give chocolate to dogs?
a: It contains a substance that is poisonous to dogs
It makes dogs tired at once
113873.e: Cocoa contains the alkaloid theobromine. People break it down quickly, but dogs only very slowly, so it can poison them.

113874.q: Which bitter alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree helped against malaria?
113874.e: Quinine is obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree. For a long time it was the most important remedy against malaria, and it gives tonic water its bitter taste.
113874.m: Quinine from cinchona bark was long the most important malaria remedy.

113875.q: Which poisonous plant with shiny black berries contains the poison atropine?
113875.e: The scientific name of deadly nightshade is Atropa belladonna. The poison atropine gets its name from it.
113875.m: Deadly nightshade contains the poison atropine.

113876.e: Atropine is a strong poison found in deadly nightshade and other members of the nightshade family.

113877.q: Which part of the body does the poison atropine mainly affect?
113877.e: Atropine disrupts the passing on of signals in the nervous system. This changes things like the heartbeat, saliva and pupils.
113877.m: Atropine acts on the nervous system.

113878.q: Which plant family does deadly nightshade belong to?
113878.e: Like the potato, deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family. Many plants in this family contain poisons.
113878.m: Deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family.

113879.q: Why should you never eat unknown berries in the forest?
a: They could be poisonous like deadly nightshade
They make you tired at once
113879.e: Some berries, such as deadly nightshade, are deadly even in small amounts. That is why you only eat berries you know for certain.

113880.q: What should you do if someone has eaten deadly nightshade berries?
a: Call Tox Info on 145 or the emergency number at once
Get them to drink lots of milk
113880.e: Deadly nightshade poisoning is life-threatening. Tox Info Suisse on 145 and the emergency number 144 can help straight away.
113880.m: In case of poisoning, call 145 or 144 at once.

113881.q: Can a poison like atropine also be useful as a medicine?
a: Yes, in a small, exact dose
113881.e: In small, exactly measured amounts, doctors use atropine as a medicine, for example as an antidote to nerve poisons. The dose makes the poison.
113881.m: The dose decides whether a substance is poisonous or healing.

113882.q: What does “belladonna”, the species name of deadly nightshade, mean in Italian?
113882.e: In the past, women dripped deadly nightshade juice into their eyes. This made their pupils large, which was seen as beautiful. But it was dangerous.

113883.q: Besides deadly nightshade, which of these plants also contains atropine?
113883.e: The thorn apple is also a member of the nightshade family and contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade. Its seeds are especially poisonous.
113883.m: The thorn apple contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade.

113884.q: In which parts of monkshood is the poison especially concentrated?
a: In the hairs on the stem
113884.e: Aconitine is in all parts of the plant. But the root tubers and the seeds contain the most.
113884.m: In monkshood, the roots and seeds are especially poisonous.

113885.q: What amount of aconitine can already be deadly for an adult?
113885.e: Just about 5 milligrams of pure aconitine can kill an adult. That is a tiny amount, much less than a gram.
113885.m: Just a few milligrams of aconitine are life-threatening.

113886.q: Which Alpine plant contains the strong poison aconitine?
113886.e: Monkshood is considered the most poisonous plant in Europe. Its poison is called aconitine.

113887.q: What should you do if you see monkshood while hiking?
a: Do not pick it and do not touch it
113887.e: The poison of monkshood can even be taken in through the skin. So it is best to leave the plant where it is.

113888.q: Which first sign is typical of aconitine poisoning?
113888.e: Aconitine disrupts the nerves. First the mouth and skin tingle, and later the skin in these places goes numb.
113888.m: Monkshood poisoning often starts with tingling and numbness.

113889.q: Which plant family does monkshood belong to?
113889.e: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family. There are many poisonous species in this family, including the buttercup itself.
113889.m: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family.

113890.q: Where does the German name of monkshood, “Eisenhut” (iron hat), come from?
a: Its flower looks like a helmet
It only grows on iron ore
Its stems are as hard as iron
113890.e: The top petal arches like a knight's helmet, which used to be called an iron hat. That is where the name comes from. The English name monkshood compares it to a monk's hood.
113890.m: The monkshood flower looks like a helmet.

113891.q: Which organ can aconitine disrupt in a life-threatening way?
113891.e: Aconitine throws the heart rhythm into confusion and paralyses breathing. A person can die from this.
113891.m: Aconitine can throw the heart out of rhythm.

113892.q: Which plant contains the poison colchicine?
113892.e: The autumn crocus contains colchicine in all its parts. The seeds and the bulb are especially poisonous.
113892.m: The poison of the autumn crocus is called colchicine.

113893.q: Which edible plant are the poisonous leaves of the autumn crocus often confused with in spring?
113893.e: The autumn crocus puts out its leaves in spring, when wild garlic is also being gathered. Its leaves contain the dangerous poison colchicine.
113893.m: The autumn crocus can be confused with wild garlic.

113894.q: Where is the ovary of the autumn crocus while it flowers in autumn?
a: At the top of the flower
113894.e: During flowering, the ovary stays protected deep in the ground. Only the following spring does the seed capsule grow upwards with the leaves.
113894.m: In the autumn crocus, the ovary stays in the ground while it flowers.

113895.q: What does colchicine block in the cells?
113895.e: Colchicine stops cells from dividing properly. That is why it mainly harms tissues that renew themselves quickly, such as the gut.
113895.m: Colchicine is a poison that stops cells dividing.

113896.q: What is true of colchicine, the poison of the autumn crocus?
a: In tiny amounts it is used as a medicine
It is used as a sweetener
113896.e: In very small, exactly measured amounts, colchicine is used for example against gout. But just a little more can be deadly.
113896.m: Colchicine is poisonous but helps as a medicine in tiny amounts.

113897.q: What is typical of the course of colchicine poisoning?
a: The symptoms only begin after hours
You feel severe pain at once
The skin turns blue at once
113897.e: First symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea often only appear a few hours after eating. That is why the danger is easily underestimated.
113897.m: Autumn crocus poisoning often only shows after hours.

113899.q: Why is the autumn crocus dangerous for cows too when it is in the hay?
a: The poison remains when it dries
The plant becomes prickly in the hay
113899.e: On the pasture, animals usually avoid the plant. But in hay they recognise it less easily, and the colchicine stays poisonous even when dried.
113899.m: Dried autumn crocus in hay stays poisonous too.

113900.q: Which tree contains the poison taxine?
113900.e: The scientific name of the yew is Taxus. That is why its poison is called taxine.
113900.m: The yew is a poisonous conifer with the poison taxine.

113901.q: How old can a yew tree become?
113901.e: The yew grows very slowly and can reach an enormous age. Some yews are well over 1,000 years old.
113901.m: Yews can live for over 1,000 years.

113902.q: Which organ does taxine mainly affect?
113902.e: Taxine disrupts the heart rhythm. In severe poisoning the heart can stop.
113902.m: The yew's poison mainly attacks the heart.

113903.q: Why do not all yew trees bear red fruits?
a: There are male and female trees
Only old yews are poisonous enough
The fruits only grow in the shade
113903.e: The yew has separate male and female trees: male and female flowers grow on different trees. Only female yews form seeds with the red seed coat.
113903.m: Only female yews bear the red fruits.

113904.q: How do yew seeds often reach new places?
a: Birds eat the fruits and drop the seeds in their droppings
The wind carries the heavy seeds far away
Bees carry the seeds into their hive
The seeds float away on rivers
113904.e: Birds eat the sweet red seed coat. They pass out the hard seed undigested and so spread the yew.
113904.m: Birds spread the seeds of the yew.

113905.q: How do roe deer react to young yew shoots?
