114265.e: A soil horizon is a horizontal layer in the soil that differs from the others in colour, grain size or humus content.
114265.m: A soil horizon is a layer in the soil.

114266.q: Which letter is used for the humus-rich topsoil?
114266.e: The topsoil is called the A horizon. It is usually dark because it contains lots of humus.
114266.m: The topsoil is the A horizon.

114267.q: Which letter is used for the subsoil?
114267.e: Below the topsoil comes the B horizon, the subsoil. It contains less humus but often weathered minerals.
114267.m: The subsoil is the B horizon.

114268.q: What does the C horizon refer to?
114268.e: The C horizon is the barely changed rock beneath the soil. The upper horizons formed from it through weathering.
114268.m: The C horizon is the rock beneath the soil.

114269.q: What does the O horizon refer to?
a: The covering of dead plant parts
114269.e: The O stands for organic. It means the covering of leaves, needles and other plant remains on top of the mineral soil.
114269.m: The O horizon consists of leaves and plant remains.

114270.q: Why is the topsoil in a field often evenly mixed?
a: Because no plants grow on it
Because it consists of pure rock
114270.e: Ploughing turns over and mixes the top layer of soil again and again. That is why it often looks even in fields.
114270.m: Ploughing mixes the topsoil of a field.

114271.q: What is another name for topsoil in German, often used for garden soil?
114271.e: In German, humus-rich topsoil is also called “Mutterboden”, mother soil. On building sites it is removed and used again later.
114271.m: “Mutterboden” is another German word for topsoil.

114272.q: In which horizon do most soil organisms live?
114272.e: In the topsoil there is plenty of food, air and roots. That is why most soil organisms live there.
114272.m: Most soil organisms live in the topsoil.

114273.q: How does humus affect the structure of the soil?
a: It sticks soil particles together into loose crumbs
It turns the soil into solid stone
It dissolves all the soil particles
It fills all the pores with water
114273.e: Humus substances bind with clay particles and stick soil particles together into crumbs. A crumbly soil is loose and well aerated.
114273.m: Humus makes the soil nice and crumbly.

114274.q: Who turns fallen leaves into humus?
a: Soil organisms such as worms, fungi and bacteria
114274.e: Earthworms, woodlice and other animals break up the leaves. Fungi and bacteria then break them down further and form humus.
114274.m: Soil organisms turn leaves into humus.

114275.q: Why is humus so important for plants?
a: It makes the soil rock hard
114275.e: Humus works like a sponge: it holds on to water and stores nutrients that plants can take up slowly.
114275.m: Humus stores water and nutrients for plants.

114276.q: Roughly how long does it take for garden waste in a compost heap to become crumbly soil?
a: A few months to about a year
114276.e: Soil organisms need time to break down vegetable peelings and leaves. Depending on warmth and moisture, the compost is ready after a few months to about a year.
114276.m: Garden waste turns into humus in a few months.

114277.q: What is released when soil organisms completely break down plant remains?
a: Nutrients that plants take up again
114277.e: During complete breakdown, called mineralisation, the nutrients from the plant remains are released again. The roots can take them up once more.
114277.m: When plant remains break down, nutrients are released again.

114278.q: How can you make humus in your own garden?
114278.e: On the compost heap, soil organisms break down vegetable peelings, grass cuttings and leaves. This produces nutrient-rich compost.
114278.m: A compost heap turns green waste into humus.

114279.q: Which chemical element does humus store in large amounts?
114279.e: Humus consists largely of carbon. That is why soils are important carbon stores for the climate.

114280.q: Which soil animal eats earth and loosens the soil with its tunnels?
114280.e: Earthworms dig tunnels through which air and water get into the soil. As they do so, they eat earth and plant remains.

114281.q: Which soil organisms are there in the greatest numbers?
114281.e: Bacteria are tiny and occur in huge numbers. Even one gram of soil contains millions to billions of them.
114281.m: Bacteria are the most common soil organisms.

114282.q: What important job do many soil organisms have?
a: They break down dead plant parts into humus
They make the soil hard and dense
They remove all the water from the soil
114282.e: Bacteria, fungi, worms and many small animals break down leaves and other remains. This creates fertile humus.
114282.m: Soil organisms turn dead plant parts into humus.

114283.q: Which living things form a partnership with plant roots called mycorrhiza?
114283.e: In mycorrhiza, fungal threads wrap around the roots. The fungus supplies water and nutrients, and the plant gives it sugar.
114283.m: In mycorrhiza, fungi and roots help each other.

114284.q: Which tiny soil animal can fling itself forward with a jumping fork?
114284.e: Springtails are only a few millimetres long. With a jumping fork on their abdomen they can jump a long way.
114284.m: Springtails jump with a jumping fork.

114285.q: Which mammal digs tunnels in the ground and eats mainly earthworms?
114285.e: The mole lives almost entirely underground. With its broad digging paws it builds tunnels and hunts worms and insect larvae in them.

114286.q: Which soil animals with very many pairs of legs often live in leaf litter?
114286.e: Millipedes have a long, segmented body with many pairs of legs. Many species eat dead plant parts and so help to break down the litter.
114286.m: Millipedes help to break down leaf litter.

114287.q: What is said about the number of living things in a handful of healthy soil?
a: There are more than there are people on Earth
There is not a single one
114287.e: Billions of tiny living things live in a handful of soil. That is more than there are people on Earth.
114287.m: A handful of soil is full of life.

a: Water freezes in cracks and expands
114288.e: Water gets into cracks and freezes. Ice takes up more space than water and so splits the rock apart.

114289.q: By roughly how much does the volume of water increase when it freezes?
114289.e: Ice has a lower density than water. When water freezes, its volume increases by around 9 per cent.
114289.m: Ice takes up about 9 per cent more space than water.

114290.q: What slowly dissolves limestone during chemical weathering?
114290.e: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic. This water dissolves limestone, which is how caves and grooved rock surfaces form in limestone mountains, for example.

114291.q: What is an example of biological weathering?
a: Ice splits a crack in a rock
114291.e: In biological weathering, living things are at work. Growing roots push cracks open, and lichens attack the rock surface.
114291.m: Plants can break up rock too.

114292.q: Which type of weathering is especially important in the high Alps?
a: Weathering by heat in the rainforest
114292.e: In the Alps it freezes and thaws very often. This means rocks are split by ice again and again.
114292.m: In the high mountains, frost splits the rocks.

114293.q: What is the pile of rock fragments at the foot of a rock face called?
114293.e: Through weathering, stones break off the rock face and fall down. There they collect to form a scree slope.
114293.m: Scree slopes form at the foot of rock faces.

114294.q: Which weathering is caused by great heat during the day and cold at night, for example in deserts?
114294.e: Rock expands in heat and contracts in cold. Over time, these stresses make the surface flake off.
114294.m: Large differences in temperature make rock break apart.

a: The removal of soil by water or wind
The growth of a new humus layer
114295.e: In soil erosion, soil particles are washed or blown away. Above all, the fertile topsoil is lost.

114296.q: What protects soil best against erosion?
114296.e: Plants hold the soil in place with their roots and slow down rain and wind. Covered soil is hardly removed at all.
114296.m: Plants protect the soil from erosion.

114297.q: Why is soil erosion especially strong on steep slopes?
a: The water runs off faster there
The ground there is always frozen
114297.e: The steeper a slope is, the faster rainwater runs off. Fast water can carry away more soil particles.
114297.m: On steep slopes water washes away more soil.

114298.q: How should you plough a field on a slope to reduce erosion?
a: Not at all, but concrete it instead
114298.e: Furrows across the slope slow down the water running off. Furrows running downhill, on the other hand, act like small channels.
114298.m: Ploughing across the slope slows the water down.

114299.q: Roughly how long does it take for one centimetre of new soil to form?
a: Around a hundred years or more
114299.e: Soil forms very slowly through weathering and humus formation. One centimetre takes around a hundred years or even longer, which is why erosion is so harmful.

114300.q: What happened in the USA in the 1930s, when the ploughed-up prairie soil was left unprotected after droughts?
a: Storms blew away huge amounts of soil
The ground froze all year round
114300.e: After droughts and intensive ploughing of the prairie, dust storms blew the dry soil away. This period is called the “Dust Bowl”.
114300.m: Unprotected, dry soil can be blown away by the wind.

114301.q: What are the terraces in steep vineyards such as those in Lavaux for?
a: They hold the soil back on the slope
They collect snow for the winter
114301.e: Terraces with retaining walls turn a steep slope into several flat steps. This means the soil is not washed away so easily.
114301.m: Terraces protect the soil on steep slopes.

114302.q: When is a field especially at risk from erosion?
a: When thick grass grows on it
When it is surrounded by a hedge
When a layer of mulch lies on it
114302.e: Without plants or mulch, raindrops beat straight onto the earth and loosen particles. That is why cover crops are often sown after the harvest.
114302.m: Bare soil is easily washed or blown away.

114303.q: What happens when soil is compacted?
a: The soil is pressed together and the pores get smaller
The soil becomes looser and airier
114303.e: During compaction the soil particles are pressed together. The spaces for air and water get smaller or disappear.
114303.m: Compaction squeezes the air out of the soil.

114304.q: What is a main cause of soil compaction in farming?
114304.e: Tractors and harvesters often weigh many tonnes. Their weight presses the soil together, especially when they drive over it often.

114305.q: When is soil compacted especially easily?
a: When there is snow on it
When it is dry and firm
114305.e: Wet soil is soft and easy to press together. That is why you should not drive heavy machinery over wet fields.

114306.q: What is a typical result of compacted soil?
114306.e: Rainwater can hardly soak into compacted soil. It collects on the surface or runs off.

114307.q: Why do roots grow badly in compacted soil?
a: There is a lack of air and space
114307.e: Roots need oxygen and spaces in order to grow. Compacted soil lacks both.

114308.q: Which measure protects soil from compaction?
a: Wide tyres with low air pressure
Narrow tyres with high air pressure
Driving on it in the rain
114308.e: Wide tyres with low air pressure spread the weight over a larger area. This means the soil is pressed together less.
114308.m: Wide tyres spread the weight better.

114309.q: Why is compaction in the subsoil especially bad?
a: It makes the soil more fertile
114309.e: The subsoil is hardly ever ploughed and is loosened by few living things. Compaction there can last for decades.
114309.m: Compacted subsoil recovers only very slowly.

114310.q: Where can you easily see compacted soil in everyday life?
a: On a freshly dug flower bed
114310.e: On a well-trodden path, lots of people always walk in the same place. The ground becomes hard and hardly any plants grow there.
114310.m: The soil on well-trodden paths is compacted.

a: The size of the soil grains
114311.e: The soil texture depends on the proportions of sand, silt and clay. These differ in grain size.
114311.m: The soil texture depends on the grain size.

114312.q: Which of these soil types has the largest grains?
114312.e: Sand grains are much larger than silt and clay particles. You can see them with the naked eye and feel them between your fingers.
114312.m: Sand has the coarsest grains in fine soil.

114313.q: Which soil type has the smallest particles?
114313.e: Clay particles are smaller than two thousandths of a millimetre. That is why clay feels smooth and sticky.

a: A mixture of sand, silt and clay
114314.e: Loam contains sand, silt and clay in similar proportions. Loamy soils are often very fertile.
114314.m: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay.

114315.q: What is typical of a sandy soil?
a: Water soaks away quickly and it dries out fast
It stores a great deal of water
It does not let any water through
114315.e: There are large pores between the large sand grains. Water flows through quickly, and nutrients are easily washed out.
114315.m: Sandy soil lets water through and dries out quickly.

114316.q: What is typical of a clay soil?
a: It holds a lot of water and is hard to work
It is loose and crumbles away
114316.e: Clay soil has many fine pores and holds on to water tightly. When wet it is sticky; when dry it becomes hard and cracked.
114316.m: Clay soil is heavy and stores lots of water.

114317.q: What is the simple method called in which you identify the soil texture by rubbing it between your fingers?
114317.e: In the finger test you rub moist soil between your fingers. Sand feels gritty, silt feels floury and clay is smooth and sticky.
114317.m: The finger test tells you the soil texture.

114318.q: What grain size do sand grains have?
114318.e: Grains up to 2 millimetres across count as sand. The lower limit is 0.05 or 0.063 millimetres, depending on the classification. Larger grains count as gravel, smaller ones as silt.
114318.m: Sand grains are at most 2 millimetres in size.

114319.q: Which plant nutrient does the N in NPK fertiliser stand for?
114319.e: N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen. It comes from the Latin name nitrogenium.

114320.q: Which plant nutrient does the P in NPK fertiliser stand for?
114320.e: P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus. Plants need it for roots and flowers, among other things.

114321.q: Which plant nutrient does the K in NPK fertiliser stand for?
114321.e: K is the chemical symbol for potassium, from its Latin name kalium. Potassium helps the plant to regulate its water balance.

114322.q: Which nutrient mainly promotes the growth of leaves and stems?
114322.e: Nitrogen is a building block of proteins and chlorophyll. With enough nitrogen, plants grow strong and green.

114323.q: What does a plant mainly need potassium for?
114323.e: Potassium controls the water balance in the plant and makes it more resistant to drought and frost.
114323.m: Potassium regulates the plant's water balance.

114324.q: What do the three numbers on a fertiliser, for example 15-15-15, mean?
a: The content of the three main nutrients in per cent
The weight of the bag in kilos
The number of plants per bag
114324.e: The numbers give the percentage of nutrients contained, in the order N, P and K. Phosphorus and potassium are given as oxides.
114324.m: The numbers on fertiliser show its nutrient content.

114325.q: What can happen if too much fertiliser gets into lakes?
a: The water becomes as salty as seawater
The lake freezes over in summer
114325.e: Excess nutrients make algae grow strongly. When they die and are broken down, the water runs short of oxygen.

114326.q: What does a plant mainly need phosphorus for?
a: For roots, flowers and its energy supply
For the green colour of its leaves alone
114326.e: Phosphorus is a building block of the energy carriers in cells. It especially promotes root growth, flowering and seed formation.

a: Dung or slurry from farm animals
A fertiliser made in a factory
114327.e: Farmyard manure is produced on the farm, for example dung and slurry. It contains nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
114327.m: Dung and slurry are farmyard manure.

114328.q: What does the pH value of a soil tell you?
a: How acidic or alkaline the soil is
How many stones are in the soil
114328.e: The pH value is a measure of acidity. It ranges from 0 for very acidic to 14 for very alkaline.
114328.m: The pH value shows how acidic a soil is.

114329.q: What pH value does a neutral soil have?
114329.e: A pH value of 7 is neutral. Values below it are acidic, values above it alkaline.
114329.m: A pH value of 7 is neutral.

114330.q: What do you call a soil with a pH value below 7?
114330.e: The lower the pH value below 7, the more acidic the soil. If it is above 7, the soil is called alkaline.
114330.m: A pH value below 7 means acidic.

114331.q: What do you spread on soil that is too acidic to raise its pH value?
114331.e: Lime neutralises acids in the soil. This raises the pH value, and many nutrients become more available to plants.
114331.m: Lime makes acidic soils less acidic.

114332.q: What is the soil under a conifer forest usually like?
114332.e: Needles decompose slowly and form acids as they do so. That is why soils under conifer forests are usually acidic.
114332.m: The soil under conifer forests is often acidic.

114333.q: Which plant likes to grow on acidic soils?
114333.e: Bilberries thrive in acidic, humus-rich soils, for example in conifer forests. They grow badly on soils rich in lime.

114334.q: How can you easily measure the pH value of soil?
114334.e: You mix soil with water and dip a test strip into it. The colour of the strip shows the pH value.
114334.m: Test strips show the pH value by their colour.

114335.q: What is the soil on limestone, for example in the Jura, usually like?
114335.e: Lime counteracts acid. Soils on limestone are therefore usually neutral to slightly alkaline.
114335.m: Soils on limestone are rarely acidic.

114336.q: Which soil type is very common in Central Europe and the Swiss Plateau?
114336.e: Brown earths are widespread in Central Europe. They are also one of the most common soil types on the Swiss Plateau.
114336.m: Brown earth is a very common soil in Switzerland.

114337.q: Where does the brown colour of brown earth come from?
a: From iron oxides formed by weathering
114337.e: During weathering, minerals containing iron are broken down. Iron oxides form, which colour the soil brown.
114337.m: Iron oxides colour brown earth brown.

114338.q: What is the process called in which the brown subsoil of brown earth forms?
114338.e: During browning, the typical brown subsoil forms through weathering. The soil type is named after this process.
114338.m: Browning gives brown earth its colour.

114339.q: What lies at the very top of a brown earth?
114339.e: At the very top lies the dark topsoil with lots of humus. Below it comes the brown subsoil and at the very bottom the rock.
114339.m: In brown earth, the dark humus soil lies on top.

114340.q: Under which natural vegetation does brown earth typically form?
114340.e: Brown earth forms where deciduous and mixed woods grow naturally. Their litter breaks down well and provides mild humus.
114340.m: Brown earth forms under deciduous and mixed woodland.

114341.q: What are brown earths especially well suited to?
114341.e: Brown earths are usually loose, well aerated and fairly rich in nutrients. That is why they are often used as fields and meadows.
114341.m: Brown earths are good soils for farming.

114342.q: In which climate do brown earths form?
114342.e: Brown earths need enough rain and moderate temperatures so that rock weathers and iron oxides form. This is the case in the temperate climate of Central Europe.
114342.m: Brown earth is a soil of the temperate climate.

114344.q: Why do only a few earthworms live in a podzol?
a: The soil contains too much lime
114344.e: Podzols are strongly acidic and poor in nutrients. Earthworms avoid such soils.
114344.m: There are hardly any earthworms in acidic podzol.

114345.q: Under which vegetation do podzols typically form?
a: Under palm trees on the beach
114345.e: Conifer needles and heather produce lots of acids as they break down. These encourage the leaching that leads to podzol.
114345.m: Podzols form under conifer forest and heath.

114346.q: In which climate do podzols mainly form?
a: In a very dry steppe climate
114346.e: Lots of rain and cool temperatures slow down the breakdown of litter and wash substances downwards. This is how podzols form, for example in Scandinavia.
114346.m: Podzols are soils of cool, moist regions.

114347.q: What is the pale, ash-grey horizon in a podzol called?
114347.e: Iron and humus have been washed out of this horizon. Mainly pale quartz sand is left behind, which is why it looks bleached.
114347.m: A podzol has an ash-grey bleached horizon.

114348.q: What does the acidic rainwater in a podzol do to the nutrients?
a: It brings them to the surface
114348.e: Acidic seeping water dissolves iron and humus substances in the upper soil. They are washed downwards, and pale, poor sand is left at the top.
114348.m: In a podzol, acidic water washes the nutrients downwards.

114349.q: Why do roots find it hard to grow deep in some podzols?
a: A hard layer in the soil blocks the way
There is always water at the bottom
114349.e: In some podzols, iron and humus cement a layer into hard hardpan. Roots can hardly get through it.
114349.m: A hard layer in a podzol holds back the roots.

114350.q: How fertile is a podzol for farming?
a: Rather poor in nutrients and not very fertile
More fertile than any brown earth
114350.e: Podzols are strongly acidic and leached. Without lots of lime and fertiliser they are not very suitable for growing crops.

114351.q: Where in Switzerland are you more likely to find podzols?
a: At higher altitudes in the Alps under conifer forest
In the Seeland on vegetable fields
On the shores of Lake Geneva in vineyards
In the city of Basel under roads
114351.e: In the Alps it is cool and moist, and conifer forests and dwarf shrubs often grow there. These conditions encourage podzols to form.
114351.m: In the Alps there are often podzols under conifer forest.

114352.q: What is the science that studies soils and their profiles called?
114352.e: Soil science, also called pedology, investigates how soils form, how they are built up and how they can be protected.

114353.q: Which components of soil come from weathered rock?
a: Mineral grains such as sand, silt and clay
114353.e: Through weathering, rock breaks down into smaller and smaller grains. Together with humus, these mineral particles make up the soil.
114353.m: Weathered rock produces the mineral grains of soil.

114450.q: Who is the first point of contact for most health problems?
a: The emergency department at the university hospital
114450.e: The family doctor looks after basic medical care. They treat many problems themselves and only refer patients on when necessary.
114450.m: For most problems, you go to the family doctor first.

114451.q: What is the letter called with which a family doctor sends a patient on to a specialist?
114451.e: With a referral, the family doctor sends a patient to a specialist. It says what needs to be investigated.
114451.m: A referral sends patients from the family doctor to a specialist.

114452.q: What is a big advantage of always going to the same family doctor?
a: She knows your whole medical history.
She is allowed to do every operation herself.
She does not need any examinations.
114452.e: If you go to the same family doctor for a long time, she knows you well. She knows about earlier illnesses, allergies and medicines.
114452.m: The family doctor knows her patients’ medical history best.

114453.q: What do you commit to with the family doctor model of Swiss health insurance?
a: Always going to your chosen family doctor first
114453.e: With the family doctor model, you always go to your chosen family doctor first, except in an emergency. In return, the premium is usually cheaper.
114453.m: With the family doctor model, you go to the family doctor first and pay a lower premium.

114454.q: Who is often the family doctor for children in Switzerland?
114454.e: Children and teenagers are often looked after by a paediatrician. She takes on the role of family doctor for them.
114454.m: For children, the paediatrician is often the family doctor.

114455.q: What is a visit by the doctor to a sick person at home called?
114455.e: On a home visit, the doctor comes to the patient’s home. This is important for people who can no longer get to the surgery.
114455.m: On a home visit, the doctor comes to the sick person’s home.

114456.q: What is a preventive check-up at the family doctor’s for?
114456.e: In a preventive check-up you are examined even if you feel healthy. This means illnesses can be found early and treated better.
114456.m: Preventive check-ups help to find illnesses early.

114457.q: Which instrument does the family doctor use to listen to the heart and lungs?
114457.e: With the stethoscope, the doctor listens to heart sounds and breathing sounds. This lets her detect pneumonia, for example.
114457.m: You listen to the heart and lungs with a stethoscope.

114458.q: Which specialist is responsible for heart diseases?
114458.e: The Greek word “kardia” means heart. Cardiologists examine and treat the heart and the circulation.
114458.m: Cardiology is the study of the heart.

114459.q: Which specialist do you go to with a bad skin rash?
114459.e: The Greek word “derma” means skin. Dermatologists treat skin diseases such as eczema or acne.
114459.m: The dermatologist is the skin doctor.

114460.q: What is an orthopaedic specialist responsible for?
114460.e: Orthopaedic specialists treat the musculoskeletal system. This includes bones, joints, ligaments and muscles.
114460.m: The orthopaedic specialist looks after the musculoskeletal system.

114461.q: What does the abbreviation ENT stand for in a specialist doctor’s title?
114461.e: An ENT doctor examines the ears, nose and throat. You go to her, for example, if you often have ear infections.
114461.m: The ENT doctor treats the ears, nose and throat.

114462.q: Which specialist treats diseases of the brain and nerves?
114462.e: The Greek word “neuron” means nerve. Neurologists treat epilepsy or migraine, for example.
114462.m: Neurology deals with the brain and nerves.

114463.q: Which specialist do you go to if you cannot see well?
114463.e: The eye doctor examines the eyes and prescribes glasses, for example. The technical term is ophthalmologist.
114463.m: For problems with sight, the eye doctor helps.

114464.q: Which specialist mainly treats children and teenagers?
114464.e: Paediatricians know all about children’s illnesses and development. The children’s doctor is called a paediatrician.
114464.m: The paediatrician is there for children and teenagers.

114465.q: What must a doctor in Switzerland do after studying medicine to become a specialist?
a: A one-year placement in a pharmacy
An exam set by the health insurer
114465.e: After their studies, young doctors work for several years in hospitals and practices. After this further training and an exam, they receive the title of specialist.
114465.m: After medical school, you become a specialist through several years of further training.

114466.q: Which specialist interprets X-rays and other images of the inside of the body?
114466.e: Radiologists are experts in imaging methods. They assess X-rays, CT and MRI scans.
114466.m: The radiologist assesses images of the inside of the body.

114467.q: What is the main task of surgery?
a: Treating diseases and injuries by operating
114467.e: Surgeons treat patients with procedures on the body. The word comes from Greek and means something like handwork.
114467.m: In surgery, healing is done by operating.

114468.q: What is the branch of surgery called that mainly deals with injuries after accidents?
114468.e: Trauma surgery (traumatology) treats broken bones and other accident injuries. In Switzerland, it is particularly in demand after skiing and cycling accidents.
114468.m: Trauma surgery treats injuries after accidents.

114469.q: Why do surgeons wear gloves, masks and sterile clothing in the operating theatre?
a: So that no germs get into the wound
So that they do not catch a cold
So that they can be recognised more easily
So that the equipment does not get dirty
114469.e: An open wound is a way in for bacteria. Sterile clothing and instruments prevent dangerous wound infections.
114469.m: In the operating theatre, everything must be sterile so that no germs get into the wound.

a: Cutting off a part of the body
114470.e: In an amputation, a badly injured finger or foot is removed, for example. Afterwards a prosthesis can help.
114470.m: In an amputation, a part of the body is cut off.

a: An operation through very small cuts
An operation that lasts several days
114471.e: In minimally invasive procedures, surgeons work through small openings with a camera and fine instruments. This is also called keyhole surgery.
114471.m: Keyhole surgery only needs small cuts.

114472.q: What do you get before a big operation so that you feel nothing and sleep?
114472.e: Under general anaesthetic you sleep deeply and feel no pain. An anaesthetist monitors your breathing and heartbeat while this happens.
114472.m: An anaesthetic makes sure you feel nothing during the operation.

114473.q: What is it called when an organ from a donor is put into the body of a sick person?
114473.e: In a transplant, a kidney or a heart is transplanted, for example. In Switzerland, the Swisstransplant foundation coordinates organ donation.
114473.m: In a transplant, a donor organ is put in.

114474.q: What must a patient give before a planned operation, after a discussion explaining it?
114474.e: The doctor explains the benefits and risks of the procedure. Only when the patient agrees may the operation go ahead, except in emergencies.
114474.m: Before an operation, the patient’s consent is needed.

114475.q: Which organ was successfully transferred from one person to another for the first time in 1967?
114475.e: In 1967, the surgeon Christiaan Barnard in South Africa transplanted a human heart for the first time. Today, heart transplants are also possible in Switzerland.
114475.m: The first heart transplant succeeded in 1967.

114476.q: What does a general anaesthetic do?
a: You sleep deeply and feel no pain.
You stay awake but cannot speak.
You are tired for a week.
114476.e: Under general anaesthetic, consciousness and the feeling of pain are switched off. This means even big operations can be carried out without pain.
114476.m: Under general anaesthetic, you sleep deeply and feel no pain.

114477.q: What is the anaesthetic called that only numbs a small area of the body?
114477.e: With a local anaesthetic, a numbing drug is injected in one place. You stay awake but feel no pain there, for example at the dentist.
114477.m: A local anaesthetic only numbs a small area.

114478.q: What does the Greek word “anaesthesia” roughly mean?
114478.e: The prefix “an” means without, and “aisthesis” means sensation. Anaesthesia switches off the feeling of pain.

114479.q: What does a pulse oximeter on the finger measure during an anaesthetic?
a: The oxygen content of the blood
114479.e: The pulse oximeter shines red light through the finger. From this it calculates the pulse and how much oxygen the blood is carrying.
114479.m: The pulse oximeter measures the oxygen in the blood.

114480.q: Who is responsible for the anaesthetic in hospital?
114480.e: The anaesthetist puts the patient under and monitors breathing and circulation throughout the operation.
114480.m: The anaesthetist is responsible for the anaesthetic.

114481.q: How were operations usually carried out before anaesthesia was invented?
a: With the patient awake and in great pain
With an injection into the leg
Not at all, operations were forbidden
114481.e: Before anaesthesia, patients had to endure operations while fully conscious. That is why surgeons worked as fast as possible. Anaesthetics only became common from the middle of the 19th century.
114481.m: Before anaesthesia, operations were very painful.

114482.q: What does the anaesthetist particularly ask about in the discussion before an anaesthetic?
114482.e: Allergies, existing illnesses and medicines affect the choice of anaesthetic. This lets the anaesthetist avoid risks.
114482.m: Before an anaesthetic, the anaesthetist checks allergies and illnesses.

114483.q: What is a tube in an anaesthetic?
114483.e: Under deep anaesthesia, you often no longer breathe enough by yourself. The tube is placed in the windpipe, and a machine takes over the breathing.
114483.m: Under anaesthetic, you are ventilated through the tube.

114484.q: Where are the rays produced in an X-ray machine?
a: In an X-ray tube, when fast electrons hit metal
In a magnet that spins quickly
In a loudspeaker with very high notes
In a light bulb with coloured glass
114484.e: In the X-ray tube, electrons are greatly accelerated. When they crash into a metal plate (anode), X-rays are produced.
114484.m: X-rays are produced when fast electrons crash into metal.

114485.q: Why do the lungs appear dark on an X-ray?
a: They contain a lot of air, which hardly stops the rays.
114485.e: Air hardly weakens X-rays at all. So a lot of radiation passes through the lungs to the detector, and this area turns dark.
114485.m: The lungs are dark on an X-ray because they contain a lot of air.

114486.q: What do you often wear during an X-ray to protect other parts of the body from the radiation?
114486.e: Lead stops X-rays very well. A lead apron protects parts of the body that are not meant to be X-rayed.
114486.m: A lead apron protects you during an X-ray.

114487.q: Where are X-rays also used outside medicine?
a: In baggage checks at the airport
114487.e: Baggage scanners at the airport X-ray suitcases. This shows what is inside without opening the case.
114487.m: At the airport, suitcases are X-rayed.

114488.q: What type of radiation are X-rays?
114488.e: Like light, X-rays are electromagnetic waves. But they have much more energy and can therefore pass through the body.

114489.q: Why are X-rays only taken when really necessary?
a: In high doses the radiation can damage cells.
The machine needs a lot of water.
You are not allowed to eat afterwards.
114489.e: X-rays are ionising and can damage the genetic material of cells. That is why the dose is kept as small as possible.
114489.m: Only X-ray when necessary, because the radiation can damage cells.

114490.q: Which injury is very often checked with an X-ray?
114490.e: An X-ray shows whether a bone is broken and how the pieces lie. Then a decision is made about a plaster cast or an operation.

114491.q: Which radiation does a computed tomography (CT) scanner use?
114491.e: In a CT scanner, an X-ray tube circles around the body. The computer works out images from many X-ray pictures.

114492.q: What kind of images does a CT scan produce?
a: Films of the heartbeat with sound
114492.e: A CT shows the body as if cut into thin slices. From these, the computer can also work out 3D views.
114492.m: A CT shows the body in cross-sectional images.

114493.q: What does the Greek word “tome” in tomography mean?
114493.e: Tomography means roughly “writing a picture of a slice”. “Tome” means cut, and “graphein” means to write.
114493.m: Tomography means making images of slices.

114494.q: Why must you lie completely still during a CT scan?
a: Otherwise the images will be blurred
Otherwise you fall into the ring
114494.e: The machine takes many pictures one after the other. If you move, the pictures do not fit together and become blurred.
114494.m: During a CT, you lie still so the images are sharp.

114495.q: Why is a contrast medium sometimes injected for a CT scan?
a: So that blood vessels and organs show up better
So that you fall asleep faster
So that the machine is quieter
114495.e: The contrast medium blocks X-rays more than the surrounding tissue does. This makes blood vessels and organs stand out more clearly.
114495.m: Contrast media make vessels and organs easier to see in the image.

114496.q: What is an advantage of CT compared with magnetic resonance imaging?
a: There is no radiation at all.
It is completely silent and takes an hour.
You do not need a computer.
114496.e: A CT scan often takes only a few minutes. That is why it is often used in emergencies, for example after a serious accident.
114496.m: A CT is quick, so it is very useful in emergencies.

114497.q: What is a disadvantage of CT compared with a single normal X-ray?
114497.e: In a CT scan, a great many X-ray pictures are taken. So you receive much more radiation than with a single picture.
114497.m: A CT gives more radiation than a simple X-ray.

114498.q: How does the patient lie during a CT scan?
a: On a couch that moves through a ring
Standing in front of a wall
114498.e: The couch slowly moves the body through the ring-shaped opening. Inside the ring, the X-ray tube rotates all the way round.
114498.m: In a CT, you move through a ring on a couch.

114499.q: What does an MRI scanner use to produce its images?
a: A strong magnetic field and radio waves
114499.e: MRI uses a very strong magnetic field and radio waves. The hydrogen nuclei in the body send out signals, from which images are calculated.
114499.m: MRI works with a magnetic field and radio waves.

114500.q: Why must you remove all metal objects before an MRI scan?
a: The strong magnetic field attracts metal.
Metal immediately gets as hot as a pan.
114500.e: The magnetic field is much stronger than a fridge magnet. Objects containing iron can fly across the room and injure people.
114500.m: In the MRI room, metal is dangerous because the magnet attracts it.

114501.q: What do patients often notice during an MRI scan?
114501.e: When the magnetic coils switch, loud knocking and humming noises are produced. That is why you are given headphones or earplugs.
114501.m: An MRI is loud, so you wear ear protection.

114502.q: What is MRI particularly good for?
a: Soft tissues such as the brain, ligaments and cartilage
114502.e: MRI shows soft tissues with very good contrast. That is why it is often used to examine knee injuries or the brain.
114502.m: MRI shows soft tissues particularly well.

114503.q: In which unit is the strength of an MRI scanner’s magnetic field given?
114503.e: The unit of magnetic flux density is called the tesla. Normal MRI scanners have 1.5 or 3 tesla, which is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s magnetic field.
114503.m: The strength of the MRI magnet is measured in tesla.

114504.q: What is a big advantage of MRI compared with CT?
114504.e: MRI works without ionising radiation. That is why it is gentle even when examinations are repeated.
114504.m: MRI does not expose the body to X-rays.

114505.q: Which Swiss chemist from ETH Zurich received the Nobel Prize in 1991 for work on nuclear magnetic resonance, which is also important for MRI?
114505.e: Richard Ernst developed nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy decisively further. His methods also helped in the development of magnetic resonance imaging.
114505.m: Richard Ernst from ETH received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991.

114506.q: What does an MRI scanner use to produce images of the inside of the body?
114506.e: MRI works with a very strong magnetic field and radio waves. Unlike X-rays, there is no harmful radiation.
114506.m: An MRI takes pictures with a strong magnetic field.

a: A tube with a camera and a light
A device for measuring blood pressure
114507.e: An endoscope is a thin, often flexible tube with a light source and a camera. It lets you look inside the body.
114507.m: With an endoscope, you look inside the body with a camera and light.

114508.q: What does the Greek word “endoscopy” roughly mean?
114508.e: “Endon” means inside, and “skopein” means to look at. So in an endoscopy, you look inside the body.

114509.q: What is an endoscopy of the stomach called?
114509.e: In a gastroscopy, the endoscope is pushed through the mouth into the gullet and stomach. This shows inflammation, for example.
114509.m: A gastroscopy is an endoscopy of the stomach.

114510.q: What does the doctor examine in an arthroscopy, for example after a sports accident?
a: The inside of a joint such as the knee
114510.e: In an arthroscopy, a thin camera is pushed into a joint, often the knee. This shows injured ligaments or cartilage.
114510.m: In an arthroscopy, you look inside the joint.

114511.q: What else can the doctor do during an endoscopy, besides looking?
114511.e: Fine forceps can be passed through a channel in the endoscope. A tissue sample (biopsy) is taken this way and examined in the laboratory.
114511.m: During an endoscopy, tissue samples can be taken.

114512.q: What carries the light round the bends in a flexible endoscope?
114512.e: In glass fibres, light is reflected back again and again at the wall (total internal reflection). This lets it travel even through bent tubes.
114512.m: Glass fibres carry light round bends.

114513.q: Which body system is examined in a bronchoscopy?
114513.e: The bronchi are the branches of the windpipe in the lungs. In a bronchoscopy, you look into the windpipe and bronchi.
114513.m: In a bronchoscopy, you look into the airways.

a: You swallow a capsule with a built-in camera.
A camera is stuck onto your skin.
You wear a camera on your head.
114514.e: The small camera capsule travels through the intestine and takes lots of photos on the way. This even makes it possible to examine the small intestine.
114514.m: In a capsule endoscopy, you swallow a mini camera.

114515.q: What do you need a doctor’s prescription for?
a: To set up a health insurance company
114515.e: The pharmacy only hands out many medicines on prescription. This ensures that a doctor has checked the treatment.
114515.m: Prescription-only medicines are only available with a prescription.

114516.q: Who is allowed to write a prescription for medicines?
114516.e: Doctors write prescriptions after examining the patient. The pharmacy then hands out the medicine.
114516.m: Prescriptions are written by the doctor.

114517.q: What is written on a prescription, among other things?
a: The name of the medicine and the dose
114517.e: The prescription states the medicine, the amount and how often to take it. It also has the patient’s name and the doctor’s stamp and signature.
114517.m: A prescription names the medicine and the dose.

114518.q: Which authority decides in Switzerland whether a medicine requires a prescription?
114518.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products in Bern. It authorises medicines and puts them into dispensing categories.

114519.q: Which medicines can you only get on a doctor’s prescription in Switzerland?
114519.e: Antibiotics are prescription-only. Taken wrongly, they can do harm and make bacteria resistant.
114519.m: Antibiotics are only available on prescription.

114520.q: What is a special feature of many doctors’ surgeries in German-speaking Switzerland?
a: Doctors may hand out medicines directly.
Prescriptions must be ordered from the Federal Council.
Medicines are only available in hospital.
114520.e: In many cantons of German-speaking Switzerland there is self-dispensing. This means you get medicines directly at the doctor’s surgery instead of at the pharmacy.
114520.m: With self-dispensing, the doctor’s surgery hands out medicines directly.

114521.q: Where do you normally take a prescription to get your medicine?
114521.e: At the pharmacy you get the prescribed medicine in exchange for the prescription. The pharmacist also explains how to take it.
114521.m: You take a prescription to the pharmacy.

a: A prescription that is valid for several collections
114522.e: People with chronic illnesses often need the same medicine for a long time. With a repeat prescription, they can collect it several times during a certain period.
114522.m: With a repeat prescription, you collect a medicine several times.

a: A copy with the same active ingredient
114523.e: A generic contains the same active ingredient in the same amount as the original medicine. It may be sold once the patent has expired.
114523.m: A generic is a copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient.

114524.q: When may a company sell a generic version of a medicine?
a: When the patent protection of the original has expired
As soon as the original is one year old
114524.e: The original medicine is protected by a patent. A patent lasts at most 20 years; after that, other companies may copy the active ingredient.
114524.m: Generics only exist after the patent has expired.

114525.q: Why are generics usually cheaper than original medicines?
a: There are no costs for expensive research and development.
They are only half as strong.
They are only sold in small packs.
114525.e: The maker of the original put a lot of money into research and studies. Generic companies do not have to, and so can sell more cheaply.
114525.m: Generics are cheaper because there are no research costs.

114526.q: In what may a generic and the original medicine differ?
a: In colour, shape and inactive ingredients
In the amount of active ingredient
114526.e: The active ingredient and its amount must be the same. Inactive ingredients such as colourings or fillers, as well as the name and appearance, may be different.
114526.m: Generics have the same active ingredient but may look different.

114527.q: What must a generic prove before it is authorised?
a: That it works in the body in the same way as the original
That it is bigger than the original
That it only works at night
114527.e: Studies show that the active ingredient gets into the blood just as quickly and strongly. This is called bioequivalence.
114527.m: A generic must work in the same way as the original.

114528.q: Why do health insurers often recommend a generic instead of the original?
a: It works the same but costs less
It is made only from plants
114528.e: A generic contains the same active ingredient as the original and works in the same way. Because it is cheaper, healthcare costs go down.
114528.m: Generics work the same and are cheaper.

114529.q: What may a pharmacist in Switzerland do in many cases if an original medicine is written on the prescription?
a: Hand out a cheaper generic instead
114529.e: Pharmacists may replace an original with a generic, unless the doctor has expressly ruled this out. This lowers healthcare costs.
114529.m: The pharmacy may often replace an original with a generic.

a: Instructions for use that come with a medicine
A letter from the doctor to the health insurer
114530.e: The package leaflet is inside the medicine packet. It contains everything important for using the medicine safely.
114530.m: The package leaflet explains how to use a medicine correctly.

114531.q: What do you find in the package leaflet of a medicine?
114531.e: The package leaflet says how much to take and when. In Switzerland it is officially called the patient information.
114531.m: The package leaflet tells you the correct dose of a medicine.

114532.q: What does the “side effects” section in the package leaflet describe?
a: Where you can buy the medicine
114532.e: As well as the desired effect, a medicine can also have unwanted effects. These side effects are listed in the package leaflet.
114532.m: Side effects are unwanted effects of a medicine.

114533.q: What does it mean when a side effect is described as “rare” in the package leaflet?
a: Only very few people get it
114533.e: “Rare” means that only a few out of many thousands of people treated are affected. So most people notice nothing of it.
114533.m: Rare side effects affect only very few people.

114534.q: What are “contraindications” in the package leaflet?
a: Situations in which you must not take the medicine
114534.e: Contraindications name cases in which the medicine could do harm, for example if you are allergic to the active ingredient.
114534.m: Contraindications say when you must not take a medicine.

114535.q: What do “interactions” in the package leaflet describe?
a: How often you should change the packet
How the weather affects the skin
114535.e: Some medicines strengthen or weaken each other. Food or alcohol can also change the effect.
114535.m: Interactions show how medicines affect each other.

114536.q: In which languages must the patient information be available in Switzerland?
114536.e: The patient information must be available in the three main national languages. This means people in all parts of the country can read it.
114536.m: The patient information is available in German, French and Italian.

114537.q: What should you do if you do not understand something in the package leaflet?
a: Ask at the pharmacy or the doctor’s
114537.e: Pharmacists and doctors answer questions about medicines. This helps to avoid mistakes when taking them.
114537.m: If anything is unclear, ask at the pharmacy or the doctor’s.

114539.q: Which aid do Rega crews use on helicopter flights at night?
114539.e: Night vision goggles amplify the little light there is. This lets the crews spot obstacles such as cables even in the dark.
114539.m: At night, Rega crews fly with night vision goggles.

114540.q: What can Rega waive for its patrons?
a: The costs of rescue missions that no insurance pays
114540.e: If no insurance covers a Rega mission, Rega can waive the costs for patrons. This is a thank-you for their support.
114540.m: Patrons often do not have to pay for uncovered Rega missions themselves.

a: Through taxes from all the cantons
114541.e: Rega is a non-profit foundation. Millions of patrons pay a contribution every year and so make its work possible.
114541.m: Patron contributions are Rega’s most important source of money.

114542.q: What does Rega use to bring patients back from far-away countries?
114542.e: For long distances, Rega uses its own air ambulance jets. They have an intensive care unit on board.
114542.m: With air ambulance jets, Rega flies sick people home from abroad.

114543.q: What is a typical task of Rega helicopters?
a: Flying injured people quickly to hospital
114543.e: Rega helicopters fly emergency doctors to accident scenes and injured people to hospitals. In the mountains especially, this is often the fastest way.
114543.m: Rega helicopters take injured people quickly to hospital.

114544.q: Where is Rega’s headquarters with the Rega Centre?
114544.e: The Rega Centre is at Zurich Airport. The operations centre, the air ambulance jets and the administration are housed there.
114544.m: Rega has its headquarters at Zurich Airport.

114545.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for a road ambulance?
114545.e: 144 is the emergency number for ambulances. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade.
114545.m: For an ambulance in Switzerland, dial 144.

114546.q: Which specialist do you go to with asthma?
114546.e: Asthma is a disease of the airways. Lung specialists, also called pulmonologists, treat the lungs and bronchial tubes.
114546.m: With asthma, the lung specialist helps.

114547.q: Why did far fewer people die after operations from about 1870 onwards?
a: Wounds and instruments were made germ-free
Operations were only done at night
114547.e: Surgeons such as Joseph Lister began to clean wounds and instruments with germ-killing substances. This meant there were far fewer wound infections.
114547.m: Working germ-free made operations much safer.

114548.q: Why does the dentist sometimes take an X-ray of your teeth?
a: To find tooth decay between the teeth
To find out the colour of the teeth
114548.e: Decay between the teeth often cannot be seen from the outside. A small X-ray shows the holes early.
114548.m: Dentists also find tooth decay with X-rays.

114549.q: What is the examination called in which a camera is used to look inside the bowel?
114549.e: In a colonoscopy, an endoscope is pushed into the large intestine. Small growths can also be removed during it.
114549.m: A colonoscopy lets doctors look inside the bowel.

114550.q: Air at 20 °C can hold at most about 17.3 g of water vapour per cubic metre. It contains 8.65 g. What is the relative humidity?
114550.e: You divide the amount present by the maximum amount: 8.65 g ÷ 17.3 g = 0.5. That is 50 per cent.
114550.m: Relative humidity is the amount present divided by the maximum amount.

114551.q: Which instrument is used to measure humidity?
114551.e: The Greek word ‘hygros’ means wet. A hygrometer usually shows relative humidity in per cent.
114551.m: Humidity is measured with a hygrometer.

114552.q: A hair hygrometer measures humidity with a hair. What does the hair do in damp air?
114552.e: Hair absorbs moisture from the air and stretches slightly. This change in length moves a pointer. The device was invented by the Geneva scientist Saussure.
114552.m: In a hair hygrometer, the hair gets longer in damp air.

114553.q: Why does the air in heated flats often become very dry in winter?
a: Cold air that is warmed up has a low relative humidity.
The heating sucks water out of the air.
In winter there is no water vapour outside.
114553.e: Cold outside air contains little water vapour. When it is warmed indoors it could hold much more, so the relative humidity drops sharply.
114553.m: Warmed winter air feels dry because its relative humidity falls.

114554.q: Why does warm weather feel ‘muggy’ when the humidity is high?
a: Sweat evaporates poorly and cools you less.
The Sun shines more strongly then.
The wind always blows harder then.
114554.e: Sweat cools the body when it evaporates. If the air is already almost saturated, it hardly evaporates and you feel sticky and hot.
114554.m: In muggy weather, sweat evaporates poorly.

114555.q: What relative humidity do most people find comfortable indoors?
114555.e: Air that is too dry irritates the eyes and the lining of the nose, air that is too damp encourages mould. That is why about 40 to 60 per cent is considered a good range.
114555.m: Indoors, about 40 to 60 per cent humidity is comfortable.

114556.q: Why does dew often form on the grass in the morning?
a: The grass cools below the dew point at night.
It always rains briefly at night.
The wind brings water from the lake.
114556.e: On clear nights the ground and plants give off heat and get cold. The air right next to them cools below the dew point and water vapour condenses.
114556.m: Dew forms when surfaces cool below the dew point.

114557.q: Why does a bottle mist up when you take it out of the fridge?
a: The air next to the cold bottle cools below the dew point.
Water seeps out through the glass.
The fridge sprays water onto it.
114557.e: The cold bottle cools the air around it. When the temperature of that air falls below the dew point, water droplets form on it.
114557.m: Water vapour from the air condenses on cold objects.

114558.q: What is true when the air temperature and the dew point are the same?
a: There is no wind at all.
It is sure to get hot.
114558.e: When the air is as cold as its dew point, it is saturated. Fog often forms then.
114558.m: When temperature and dew point match, the air is saturated.

114559.q: A rule of thumb says: cloud base in metres is roughly 125 times (temperature minus dew point). At ground level it is 20 °C and the dew point is 12 °C. Roughly how high is the cloud base?
114559.e: The difference is 20 minus 12 = 8 degrees. 8 × 125 m = 1000 m.
114559.m: The bigger the gap to the dew point, the higher heap clouds form.

114560.q: Why do your glasses mist up when you come into a warm room in winter?
a: The cold lenses cool the warm room air below the dew point.
The air in the room is drier than outside.
114560.e: The lenses are still cold from outside. The damp room air cools below the dew point on them, and droplets form.
114560.m: Cold glasses mist up in warm air.

114561.q: What happens to the dew point when the air contains more water vapour?
114561.e: Damper air is already saturated at a higher temperature. That is why its dew point is higher.
114561.m: The damper the air, the higher its dew point.

114562.q: Why does rising air cool down?
a: It expands as the air pressure falls.
It gets closer to the cold Sun.
It is cooled by the wind.
114562.e: Higher up the air pressure is lower, so the air expands. In doing so it uses energy and cools down.
114562.m: Rising air expands and cools as it does so.

114563.q: Roughly how much does dry rising air cool for every 100 metres it climbs?
114563.e: Unsaturated air cools by about 1 °C per 100 m as it rises. This is called dry adiabatic cooling.
114563.m: Dry air cools by about one degree per hundred metres as it rises.

114564.q: An unsaturated parcel of air at 18 °C rises 800 m. Roughly what temperature does it have afterwards?
114564.e: It cools by about 1 °C per 100 m, so by 8 °C. 18 °C minus 8 °C = 10 °C.
114564.m: For every hundred metres it rises, dry air gets about one degree colder.

114565.q: What do water droplets need in order to form in a cloud?
114565.e: Water vapour condenses on tiny particles such as dust, soot or salt crystals. Without these condensation nuclei, hardly any droplets would form.
114565.m: Cloud droplets form on tiny condensation nuclei.

114566.q: What are the white heap clouds that form on fine summer days called?
114566.e: The Latin word ‘cumulus’ means heap. These clouds form when warm air rises from the ground.

114567.q: What are the high, thin cirrus clouds made of?
114567.e: Cirrus clouds are very high up, where it is very cold. That is why they are made of ice crystals and look wispy.
114567.m: Cirrus clouds are made of ice crystals.

114568.q: Which language do cloud names such as cumulus, stratus and cirrus come from?
114568.e: In 1802 the Englishman Luke Howard gave the clouds Latin names. ‘Cumulus’ means heap, ‘stratus’ layer and ‘cirrus’ curl.

114569.q: Why do thick clouds often look grey or dark from below?
a: Little sunlight gets through the thick cloud.
The sky behind them is black.
114569.e: The many droplets scatter the light in all directions. With thick clouds only a little light reaches the bottom.
114569.m: Thick clouds look dark because little light gets through.

114570.q: What happens on the windward side of the Alps during a foehn?
a: The air rises and it often rains.
The air sinks and gets warm.
There is no wind at all.
114570.e: On the windward side the air has to rise, cools and forms clouds. It often rains or snows heavily there.
114570.m: During a foehn it often rains heavily on the windward side.

114571.q: Why is the air warmer after rising over the mountains and sinking again in a foehn?
a: It cools more slowly while rising in the cloud than it warms while sinking.
The Sun only heats the lee side.
The wind rubs against the rocks.
114571.e: In the cloud, heat is released by condensation, so the air only cools by about 0.5 °C per 100 m. As it sinks dry, it warms by about 1 °C per 100 m.
114571.m: Foehn air is warm because it warms faster as it sinks than it cooled as it rose.

114572.q: Dry foehn air is 5 °C on a pass at 2500 m. It sinks to 500 m. Roughly how warm is it then?
114572.e: It sinks 2000 m and warms by about 1 °C per 100 m, so by 20 °C. 5 °C + 20 °C = 25 °C.
114572.m: Sinking dry air warms by about one degree per hundred metres.

114573.q: What is the foehn that blows on the northern side of the Swiss Alps called?
114573.e: In a south foehn the air flows over the Alps from the south and drops into the valleys on the northern side. Typical foehn valleys are the Reuss valley and the Hasli valley.
114573.m: The south foehn blows on the northern side of the Alps.

114574.q: How does the relative humidity in an Alpine valley change when the foehn starts?
a: It jumps between 0 and 100 % every minute.
114574.e: The sinking foehn air warms up a lot without taking in water vapour. That is why the relative humidity often falls below 30 per cent.
114574.m: During a foehn, the air in the valley becomes very dry.

114576.q: How can you often recognise a foehn from far away on the Swiss Plateau?
a: The mountains look very near and clear.
The sky is full of fog.
114576.e: Foehn air is very dry and clear. That is why the Alps look unusually sharp and seem close.
114576.m: During a foehn the mountains seem close enough to touch.

114577.q: Which type of cloud do thunderstorms come from?
114577.e: A cumulonimbus is a towering heap cloud. It can grow to more than 10 km high.

114578.q: What ingredients does a thunderstorm need?
a: Damp, warm air and strong rising
Dry, cold air and no wind
114578.e: Warm, damp air rises strongly and forms tall clouds. When it condenses, heat is released, which drives the air even higher.
114578.m: Thunderstorms need warm, damp air that rises strongly.

114579.q: Why do heat thunderstorms usually happen in the afternoon or evening?
a: By then the Sun has heated the ground strongly.
In the afternoon the Moon is closest.
In the morning the air is too damp.
In the evening the air pressure is highest.
114579.e: During the day the Sun heats the ground and the air near it. The warm air rises and forms thunderclouds in the afternoon.
114579.m: Heat thunderstorms usually form after strong heating in the afternoon.

114580.q: What is the flat, wide top of a thundercloud called?
114580.e: The rising air hits a warmer layer of air at the top and spreads out sideways. This creates the shape of a blacksmith's anvil.
114580.m: The top of a thundercloud looks like an anvil.

114581.q: What creates the electric charge in a thundercloud?
a: Collisions between ice and soft hail particles
114581.e: In the updraughts, ice crystals and soft hail pellets collide and swap charge. Light particles carry one charge upwards, heavy ones the other downwards.
114581.m: Thunderclouds become charged through colliding ice particles.

114582.q: What do you call a thunderstorm that forms along an approaching cold front?
114582.e: The heavy cold air pushes under the warm air and lifts it. This often creates thunderstorms in a long line.
114582.m: Frontal thunderstorms form when a cold front lifts warm air.

114583.q: Apart from lightning, what is a dangerous side effect of thunderstorms?
114583.e: Cold, rain-cooled air rushes down out of the cloud and spreads out along the ground. These gusts can blow trees over.

114584.q: Roughly how high can thunderclouds reach in Switzerland?
114584.e: Thunderclouds grow up to the upper limit of the weather, the tropopause. In our latitudes it is at about 10 to 12 km.
114584.m: Thunderclouds reach up to the tropopause.

114585.q: Why do you see lightning before you hear the thunder?
a: Light is much faster than sound.
The thunder is only made later.
The sound has to warm up first.
114585.e: Light travels about 300,000 km per second, sound only about 340 m. That is why the thunder arrives later.
114585.m: Light is much faster than sound.

114586.q: What does the speed of sound in air mainly depend on?
114586.e: In warm air the air particles move faster and pass the sound on more quickly. That is why the rule of thumb for the distance of a thunderstorm is only an estimate.
114586.m: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air.

114587.q: Which simple rule helps you estimate how many kilometres away a thunderstorm is?
a: Seconds between lightning and thunder divided by 3
114587.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. If you divide the seconds you counted by 3, you get roughly the kilometres.
114587.m: Seconds between lightning and thunder divided by three gives the distance in kilometres.

114588.q: You count 12 seconds between lightning and thunder. Roughly how far away is the lightning (sound 340 m/s)?
114588.e: 340 m/s × 12 s = 4080 m. That is about 4 km.
114588.m: Distance is the speed of sound times the time.

114589.q: You should take shelter if there are less than 30 seconds between lightning and thunder. How far away is the storm then at most?
114589.e: Using the rule of thumb, you divide the seconds by 3: 30 ÷ 3 = 10. Lightning can strike that far ahead of a storm.
114589.m: With less than thirty seconds between lightning and thunder, the storm is less than ten kilometres away.

114590.q: Lightning strikes 2 km away. Roughly how many seconds later do you hear the thunder (sound 340 m/s)?
114590.e: 2000 m ÷ 340 m/s ≈ 5.9 s. So you hear the thunder after about 6 seconds.
114590.m: Sound takes about six seconds to travel two kilometres.

114591.q: The time between lightning and thunder gets shorter with each flash. What does that mean?
114591.e: The closer the lightning, the shorter the path of the sound. If the gaps get shorter, you should take shelter at once.
114591.m: If the gaps between lightning and thunder get shorter, the storm is coming closer.

114592.q: Why can you ignore the travel time of the light when working out the distance of a storm?
a: The light is swallowed by clouds.
Light and sound are equally fast.
114592.e: Light takes only a few millionths of a second to travel a few kilometres. Compared with sound, this time is tiny.
114592.m: You see the flash of lightning practically at the same moment.

114593.q: Why can hailstones grow so big in the cloud?
a: Strong updraughts carry them up again and again.
They fall very slowly like feathers.
They get even bigger on the ground.
114593.e: In a thundercloud, powerful updraughts keep the ice pellets floating for a long time. More and more supercooled water droplets freeze onto them.

114594.q: What often suffers great damage in hailstorms in Switzerland?
114594.e: Large hailstones dent cars, smash roof tiles and destroy fruit and vegetables. Hailstorms are among the most expensive natural events in Switzerland.
114594.m: Hail causes great damage to cars, buildings and crops.

114595.q: What is often the core that a hailstone grows around?
a: A soft hail pellet or frozen droplet
A salt crystal from the sea
114595.e: A hailstone usually starts as a small soft hail pellet or frozen droplet. More and more water droplets freeze onto it in the cloud.
114595.m: A hailstone grows from a small core of ice.

114596.q: When does a hailstone fall out of the cloud?
a: When it gets too heavy for the updraughts
As soon as it gets dark
Only when the wind stops completely
114596.e: As long as the updraught is strong enough, the stone stays up. When it gets too heavy, it falls to the ground.
114596.m: A hailstone falls when the updraught can no longer carry it.

114597.q: How do fruit growers in Switzerland often protect their trees from hail?
114597.e: Nets are stretched over the orchards. They catch the hailstones before they damage fruit and leaves.
114597.m: Hail nets protect fruit from hail damage.

114598.q: Why does hail stay frozen until it reaches the ground, even on warm summer days?
a: It falls fast and is big enough not to melt completely.
The air under thunderstorms is always below 0 °C.
It is cooled again as it falls.
114598.e: Large hailstones fall through the warm air at high speed. They melt a little, but still reach the ground as ice.
114598.m: Large hailstones fall too fast to melt completely.

114599.q: What are the tiny water droplets in a cloud called that stay liquid below freezing and freeze onto the hailstone?
114599.e: Very small, clean droplets can stay liquid far below 0 °C. When they touch an ice pellet, they freeze at once.
114599.m: Supercooled droplets freeze instantly onto the hailstone.

114600.e: The Earth turns away underneath moving air. Seen from the Earth, the air therefore seems to be pushed sideways.
114600.m: The Coriolis force comes from the Earth's rotation.

114601.q: In which direction does the Coriolis force turn winds in the northern hemisphere?
114601.e: In the northern hemisphere every movement is turned to the right, seen in the direction of travel. In the southern hemisphere it is the other way round.
114601.m: In the northern hemisphere, winds are turned to the right.

114602.q: In which direction does the Coriolis force turn winds in the southern hemisphere?
114602.e: In the southern hemisphere the deflection is reversed. That is why tropical storms there also spin the other way.
114602.m: In the southern hemisphere, winds are turned to the left.

114603.q: Where is the Coriolis force on winds weakest?
114603.e: The deflecting effect depends on the latitude. At the equator it is zero, at the poles it is greatest.
114603.m: At the equator, there is no Coriolis force on horizontal winds.

114604.q: Does the Coriolis force decide which way the water drains out of the bath?
a: No, it is far too weak for that.
Yes, but only at the equator.
114604.e: The Coriolis force only has a noticeable effect over large distances and long times. In a basin, the shape and small currents decide the direction of the swirl.
114604.m: In a sink, the Coriolis force plays practically no role.

114605.q: Why do hardly any tropical storms form right at the equator?
a: There is no Coriolis force there to spin the air into a vortex.
The sea is too cold there.
The air is too dry there.
114605.e: A tropical storm needs a spinning motion, which the Coriolis force sets off. At the equator it is zero, so hardly any tropical storms form there.
114605.m: Without the Coriolis force, no tropical storm forms.

114606.e: Air warmed by the ground is lighter than the air around it and rises. These updraughts are called thermals.
114606.m: A thermal is rising warm air.

a: It has a lower density than colder air.
It is heavier than cold air.
It is attracted by the Sun.
114607.e: Warm air expands, so a cubic metre of it has less mass. The denser, colder surrounding air pushes it upwards.
114607.m: Warm air rises because it is less dense.

114608.q: Over which surface is a thermal most likely to form on a sunny day?
114608.e: Dark, dry surfaces heat up quickly in the sun. The air above them gets warm and rises.
114608.m: Dark, dry surfaces create good thermals.

114609.q: Who uses thermals to gain height without an engine?
114609.e: Paragliders and gliders circle in the updraughts. This way they climb without needing an engine.
114609.m: Glider and paraglider pilots climb in thermals.

114610.q: Which birds often circle in thermals without flapping their wings?
114610.e: Large soaring birds save a lot of energy this way. On their way to Africa, storks travel from updraught to updraught.
114610.m: Storks and birds of prey use thermals to soar.

114611.q: What often marks the top of a thermal?
114611.e: The rising air cools until its water vapour condenses. A heap cloud forms there.
114611.m: A heap cloud often forms above a thermal.

114612.q: At what time of day are thermals usually strongest on a summer day?
a: Early in the morning before sunrise
114612.e: The Sun heats the ground for hours. In the early afternoon the difference between the ground and the air is greatest.
114612.m: Thermals are strongest in the afternoon.

114613.q: Which kind of heat transfer is at work in a thermal?
114613.e: In convection, a flowing substance carries heat along with it. In a thermal, the rising air carries the heat upwards.
114613.m: A thermal is a form of convection.

114614.q: What is special about an inversion?
a: It is warmer higher up than lower down.
114614.e: Normally it gets colder the higher you go. In an inversion, a warmer layer lies on top of cold air.
114614.m: In an inversion it is warmer higher up than below.

114615.q: What does the Latin word ‘inversio’ mean?
114615.e: In an inversion, the normal pattern of temperatures is turned around. Instead of getting colder, it gets warmer with height.

114616.q: What weather is common on the Swiss Plateau in winter during an inversion?
114616.e: Cold, damp air collects on the Swiss Plateau and is covered by warmer air. A grey blanket of low cloud forms.
114616.m: In winter, inversions often bring low cloud to the Swiss Plateau.

114617.q: What do you often experience during an inversion when you go up a mountain like the Rigi?
a: Sunshine above a sea of fog
Thick fog up to the summit
114617.e: Above the inversion the air is dry and mild. From up there you look down on the white blanket of fog, the sea of fog.
114617.m: Above an inversion the Sun often shines over the sea of fog.

114618.q: Why is air quality often poor during an inversion?
a: The warm layer acts like a lid and exhaust fumes stay below.
The Sun produces extra exhaust fumes.
The fog is made of smoke.
Trees give off poison in the cold.
114618.e: The air cannot rise and mix. Fine dust and exhaust fumes collect in the cold layer near the ground.
114618.m: During an inversion, pollution stays trapped near the ground.

114619.q: Which kind of pressure system often causes inversions in winter?
114619.e: In a high, the air sinks and warms up as it does so. At the same time, the air near the ground cools strongly during long nights.
114619.m: Winter inversions often form under high pressure.

114620.q: Down in Zurich it is 0 °C, on a mountain at 1500 m it is 8 °C. What is happening?
114620.e: Normally it would be much colder higher up. If it is warmer up there, the temperature pattern is turned around.
114620.m: If it is warmer on the mountain than in the valley, there is an inversion.

114621.q: Which wind on the Swiss Plateau often comes together with low cloud in winter?
114621.e: The Bise is a cold north-east wind between the Jura and the Alps. In high-pressure weather it often blows under a blanket of low cloud.
114621.m: The Bise often blows under the low cloud.

a: Air flows from high to low air pressure.
114622.e: Differences in air pressure tend to even out. That is why air flows from a high to a low.
114622.m: Wind is air flowing from a high to a low.

114623.q: When does the wind blow harder?
a: When the difference in air pressure is bigger
When the air pressure is the same everywhere
114623.e: A big difference in pressure over a short distance pushes the air strongly. On weather maps the isobars are then close together.
114623.m: The bigger the pressure difference, the stronger the wind.

114624.q: Why is the weather often fine in a high-pressure area?
a: The air sinks, warms up and clouds dissolve.
The air rises and forms clouds.
The wind blows all the clouds into the sea.
The Sun is closer to the Earth then.
114624.e: In a high, air sinks slowly and gets warmer. Its relative humidity falls, so the clouds disappear.
114624.m: In a high the air sinks, which is why it is often sunny.

114625.q: On a clear night at a large lake, where does the wind on the shore usually come from?
a: From the land towards the lake
From the lake towards the land
Nowhere, there is never wind at night
114625.e: At night the land cools faster than the water. Air rises over the warmer lake, and cool air flows in from the land (land breeze).
114625.m: At night the wind blows from the land towards the lake.

114626.q: What weather does a low-pressure area often bring?
114626.e: In a low, air rises, cools and forms clouds. Rain or snow often falls from them.
114626.m: Low-pressure areas often bring clouds and rain or snow.

114627.q: Why does the wind usually blow harder over an open lake than in a town?
a: There are fewer obstacles and less friction.
The air pressure over water is always the same.
There is no air pressure in towns.
114627.e: Buildings and trees slow the wind through friction. Over a smooth water surface the air can flow almost freely.
114627.m: Over smooth surfaces like lakes, the wind is slowed less.

114628.q: What is the wind that blows up a mountain valley during the day called?
114628.e: The Sun warms the slopes and the air rises up the slope. Air flows in from the valley. At night it reverses, and then the mountain wind blows.
114628.m: During the day the valley wind blows up the valley.

114629.q: In how many danger levels does MeteoSwiss warn of severe weather?
114629.e: The warning levels go from 1 (no or low danger) to 5 (very high danger). They apply, for example, to thunderstorms, wind, rain or heat.
114629.m: MeteoSwiss warns in five danger levels.

114630.q: What does MeteoSwiss regularly send up in Payerne to measure the atmosphere?
114630.e: In Payerne, weather balloons carrying a radiosonde go up. They measure temperature, humidity and wind up to more than 30 km high.
114630.m: In Payerne, weather balloons with radiosondes go up.

114631.q: Where in Switzerland was the highest official temperature measured in 2003?
a: On the southern side of the Alps
114631.e: On 11 August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono in the Mesolcina valley. The southern side of the Alps is often warmer than the rest of Switzerland.
114631.m: The Swiss heat record comes from the southern side of the Alps.

114632.q: In which village in the Jura was the lowest temperature at an official Swiss weather station, minus 41.8 °C, measured in 1987?
114632.e: The high valley of La Brévine is also called the ‘Siberia of Switzerland’. On clear nights cold air collects there on the valley floor.
114632.m: La Brévine is known as the coldest place in Switzerland.

114633.q: What is a weather model at MeteoSwiss used for?
a: A computer uses it to calculate how the weather will develop.
It is used to build small wooden houses.
It is a game for children.
It measures the temperature in the garden directly.
114633.e: Weather models solve physics equations for air pressure, temperature, wind and humidity. Supercomputers use them to calculate the forecasts.
114633.m: Weather forecasts are calculated with computer models.

114634.q: What is the foehn in the Alps?
a: A warm, dry wind blowing down the mountains
A cold north wind with snow
A damp fog in the valley
114634.e: In a foehn, air flows over the Alps and drops into the valley on the other side. It becomes warm and dry as it does so.
114634.m: The foehn is a warm, dry wind blowing down the mountains.

114635.q: In which unit is absolute humidity given?
a: Grams of water vapour per cubic metre of air
114635.e: Absolute humidity tells you how many grams of water vapour there are in a cubic metre of air. Relative humidity, on the other hand, is given in per cent.
114635.m: Absolute humidity is measured in grams per cubic metre.

114636.q: Why do glider pilots often fly in circles in an updraught?
a: So that they stay in the updraught and climb
So that they don't get dizzy
So that they scare birds away
114636.e: A thermal updraught is often only a few hundred metres wide. If you circle inside it, you stay in the rising air and gain height.
114636.m: Glider pilots circle to stay in the thermal.

114638.q: What do many plants do first during a drought to save water?
114638.e: Water evaporates through the tiny pores (stomata) on the leaves. In a drought they close so that less water is lost.
114638.m: In a drought, plants close their stomata.

114639.q: Why do plants hardly grow at all under severe drought stress?
a: Little carbon dioxide gets into the leaf
114639.e: The leaf also takes in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis through the stomata. When they are closed, the plant makes hardly any sugar and so hardly grows.
114639.m: Without carbon dioxide a plant can hardly carry out photosynthesis.

114640.q: Which soil stores water best for plants in dry periods?
114640.e: Loam and humus hold water in fine pores like a sponge. Water, on the other hand, seeps quickly down through sand and gravel.
